cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 330"><text class="t-bold" x="30" y="60" text-anchor="start">T1</text><text class="t-bold" x="30" y="150" text-anchor="start">T2</text><line class="s-line w1" x1="60" y1="50" x2="620" y2="50"/><line class="s-line w1" x1="60" y1="140" x2="620" y2="140"/><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="70" y="62" width="175" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="157.5" y="92" text-anchor="middle">COUNT = 3</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="253" y="152" width="175" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="340.5" y="182" text-anchor="middle">insert row, commit</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="436" y="62" width="175" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="523.5" y="92" text-anchor="middle">COUNT = 4</text><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="255" text-anchor="middle">Phantom read: the same query gave 3 rows, then 4.</text><text class="t-small" x="320" y="285" text-anchor="middle">A committed insert arrived between the two queries.</text></svg>

reveal.text: A phantom is the same idea for a range of rows, where the set itself changes.

lead.text: Two doctors, Alice and Bob, are on call, and the rule is that at least one must remain. Each transaction checks that the count on call is 2, concludes that it is safe to leave, and updates its own row. They update *different* rows, so neither blocks the other, and both commit. Zero doctors are now on call. Each transaction was correct for the data it saw, and the failure comes from the combination, which no serial order allows: whichever went second would have seen a count of 1 and refused.

This pattern is **write skew**. It is the anomaly that Berenson and colleagues drew attention to in 1995, when they showed that the ANSI SQL definitions of isolation levels were ambiguous and did not mention it. It matters because the usual protection, a snapshot of the data for each transaction, does not prevent it.

diagram.alt: Two transactions, Alice's and Bob's, each check that two doctors are on call and then take themselves off call. After both commit, no doctor is on call, which breaks the rule that one must stay.
diagram.caption: Write skew with two doctors. Use the buttons to see the checks and then the updates.

cases.label: Both check
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 310"><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="36" text-anchor="middle">Rule: at least one doctor must stay on call</text><text class="t-bold" x="30" y="80" text-anchor="start">T1 (Alice)</text><text class="t-bold" x="330" y="80" text-anchor="start">T2 (Bob)</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="30" y="92" width="280" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="170" y="122" text-anchor="middle">count on call: 2, so Alice can leave</text><rect class="f-sunken s-line w1" x="330" y="92" width="280" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="470" y="122" text-anchor="middle">count on call: 2, so Bob can leave</text><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="200" text-anchor="middle">Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot, with 2 on call.</text><text class="t-small" x="320" y="232" text-anchor="middle">Neither sees the other's change, because neither has made one yet.</text></svg>

cases.label: Both leave
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 310"><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="36" text-anchor="middle">Rule: at least one doctor must stay on call</text><text class="t-bold" x="30" y="80" text-anchor="start">T1 (Alice)</text><text class="t-bold" x="330" y="80" text-anchor="start">T2 (Bob)</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w3" x="30" y="92" width="280" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="170" y="122" text-anchor="middle">update Alice: off call, commit</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w3" x="330" y="92" width="280" height="50" rx="6"/><text class="t-small" x="470" y="122" text-anchor="middle">update Bob: off call, commit</text><text class="t-small" x="320" y="200" text-anchor="middle">They updated different rows, so neither blocked the other.</text><text class="t-big t-bold t-warn" x="320" y="240" text-anchor="middle">On call now: 0</text><text class="t-small" x="320" y="276" text-anchor="middle">The rule is broken, although each transaction kept it on its own.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The rule was broken even though each transaction followed it, which is the mark of write skew.

lead.text: PostgreSQL offers three levels. **Read Committed** is the default, and each statement sees the data committed when it began, so it allows non-repeatable reads, phantoms and lost updates. **Repeatable Read** gives the whole transaction one snapshot, which prevents non-repeatable and phantom reads, and a transaction that tries to update a row changed since its snapshot is aborted, so a lost update is prevented as well. It still allows write skew. **Serializable** prevents every anomaly in the figure.

Higher isolation is not free. To prevent write skew, Serializable may abort a transaction with a serialisation failure, and the application must catch the error and *retry* the whole transaction. The levels follow the PostgreSQL documentation, and other databases differ, so check the one you use.

afterFigure.text: In the SQL standard, Repeatable Read may allow phantom reads, but the PostgreSQL implementation does not.

diagram.alt: A table for each of PostgreSQL's three isolation levels, listing whether dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update and write skew can happen. Only Serializable prevents all five. Read Uncommitted behaves as Read Committed.
diagram.caption: What each PostgreSQL isolation level allows. Use the buttons to compare the three levels.

steps.headline: Choose the isolation level for the doctors-on-call rule.

workedSteps.text: Name the anomaly. Two transactions read the same count and update different rows, which is write skew.
Read Committed and Repeatable Read both allow it, so neither protects the rule.
Serializable prevents it, but it may abort one of the transactions with a serialisation failure, and the application has to respond to that.
Run the aborted transaction again. It now sees the other doctor's change, finds a count of 1, and refuses to leave.

reveal.text: The database turned silent data loss into a visible error that the application can handle.

lessons.orientation: Name the anomaly in an interleaved schedule, and say which isolation levels allow it in PostgreSQL.
lessons.nextAction: Say what a transaction sees under multiversion concurrency, resolve a deadlock, and detect a conflicting update with a version column.

blocks.text: The value x is 100, and two transactions each read it and add to it, one adding 10 and the other adding 20. Run one after the other they give 130, whichever goes first, because the second starts from the value the first has left.

Run at the same time, the two overlap, and the order in which their reads and writes interleave decides what x ends up holding. Some interleavings give a result that no serial order could, and these are the anomalies.

diagram.alt: Two lanes, T1 and T2, that each read a value x equal to 100 and are about to add to it. T1 will add 10 and T2 will add 20.
diagram.caption: Two transactions that each read x and will write a new value. Use the buttons to see the first steps.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the anomaly in an interleaved schedule, and say which of PostgreSQL's isolation levels allow it.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing an isolation level is choosing which of these anomalies your application can live with.

recap.keyIdea: An isolation level promises which interleaving anomalies cannot happen, and in PostgreSQL only Serializable rules out all of them, at the price of retries.

blocks.text: Lost update, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read and write skew are each a result that no serial order would give. PostgreSQL never allows a dirty read, Repeatable Read also stops the next two and aborts a lost update, and only Serializable stops write skew.
Stronger isolation can abort a transaction with a serialisation failure, so the application must be written to retry.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how PostgreSQL gives each transaction its view of the data, and at locks and version columns.

lessons.title: Locks, versions and conflicts

reveal.text: The reader gets the old value without waiting, and the writer is not slowed by the reader.

lead.text: If every reader had to wait for every writer, a long report would stop all payments for as long as it ran. PostgreSQL avoids this with **multiversion concurrency control**, usually shortened to **MVCC**. An `UPDATE` does not overwrite a row. It creates a *new version* and marks the old one as ended by the updating transaction, so the row has a chain of versions, each recording the transaction that created it and the one that ended it.

A transaction reads through a **snapshot**, which records which transactions had committed when it started. It sees the latest version created by a committed transaction and not yet ended by one. In the figure, tx 10 created version 1 and tx 20 created version 2. A snapshot taken while tx 20 was still running sees version 1, and one taken after tx 20 committed sees version 2. A plain `SELECT` takes no row locks, and the rule that follows is that readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.

diagram.alt: The same row with two versions. In the first view a reader's snapshot was taken while transaction 20 was still running, and the reader sees version 1 with balance 100. In the second view the snapshot was taken after transaction 20 committed, and the reader sees version 2 with balance 150.
diagram.caption: Which version a snapshot sees. Use the buttons to move the snapshot before and after the commit of transaction 20.

The reader sees 150.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The same row gave two different answers to two readers, and each answer was consistent for its own snapshot.

lead.text: MVCC lets readers and writers coexist, but two writers cannot change the same row at once. An `UPDATE` takes a **row lock** on the rows it changes and holds it until the transaction ends, so a second writer to the same row waits until the first commits or rolls back.

Waiting can go wrong. Suppose T1 locks row 1 and then wants row 2, while T2 locks row 2 and then wants row 1. Each waits for a lock the other holds, which is a **deadlock**. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, and the usual cure is for every transaction to lock rows in the *same order*, which removes the cycle, with retry as the fallback.

diagram.alt: Two transactions and two rows. In the first view T1 holds row 1 and waits for row 2, while T2 holds row 2 and waits for row 1, which is a deadlock. In the second view both transactions lock row 1 first, so T2 waits for T1 and no cycle forms.
diagram.caption: The same two transactions with different lock orders. Use the buttons to compare them.

reveal.text: Waiting for a lock is normal, and it becomes a deadlock only when the waits go round in a circle.

lead.text: The lost update of the last lesson came from a gap: the application read a value with one statement, computed a new one, and wrote it with another, and any other transaction could change the row between them. Under MVCC the `SELECT` holds no lock and shows only its snapshot, so nothing stops it. There are three ways to close the gap. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the rows as it reads them, so a competing writer waits. A higher isolation level aborts the second writer. And the simplest is to do the arithmetic in the database, as in `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 7`.

The atomic UPDATE works because it takes the row lock first, and at Read Committed a waiting transaction re-evaluates the new value once the lock is released. With two such updates, one adding 10 and one adding 20, the second waits for the first and then adds to its result, so a starting value of 100 ends at 130, as in a serial order.

reveal.text: The change in where the arithmetic happens is what closes the gap.

lead.text: Sometimes holding a lock is not possible, for instance when a person opens a form, edits it for ten minutes and then saves. The **optimistic** approach hopes there is no conflict, and checks at the end. The row carries a **version column**, which the application reads along with the data and sends back in the update: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 150, version = 4 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3`.

If nobody has changed the row, its version is still 3, the statement updates 1 row and the version becomes 4. If someone else has already moved the version to 4, the `WHERE` clause matches nothing, and the statement reports **0 rows** updated. That count is the signal of a conflict: the application re-reads the row, applies its change to the new data, and tries again with the new version.

reveal.text: The update did not fail with an error. The count of rows is how the application finds out.

steps.headline: Follow two users who edit account 7, balance 100 and version 3, at the same time.

workedSteps.text: Both read the row and see balance 100 and version 3. Neither holds any lock.
User 1 saves 150 with `SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3`. The version matches, so 1 row is updated.
User 2 saves 130 with the same `WHERE version = 3`. The row is now at version 4, so 0 rows are updated.
User 2 re-reads the row, which is now at balance 150 and version 4, applies the change again and retries with `version = 4`.

steps.headline: Finish the retry for user 2, who wants to add 30.

workedSteps.text: The first attempt matched 0 rows, so user 2 re-reads the row and gets balance 150 and version 4.
User 2 adds 30 to the re-read balance and saves with `version = 4`, which matches.
User 2's change is an addition of 30 to whatever balance the row holds.

reveal.text: An alternative is a version column, which detects the conflict at the save and asks the second user to retry.

lessons.orientation: Say what a transaction sees under multiversion concurrency, resolve a deadlock, and use a version column to detect a conflicting update.

blocks.text: In PostgreSQL an UPDATE does not overwrite a row. It writes a second version of the row beside the first and marks the first as ended by the updating transaction, so while the update is in progress the same row exists in two versions at once.

The effect is that a long report can read a million rows without stopping the payments that change them. What remains are conflicts between two writers of the same row, and between a read and the write that follows it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which version a snapshot sees, resolve a deadlock, and detect a conflicting update with a version column.
intro.whyItMatters: Most concurrency bugs are a read followed by a write, and each tool in this lesson closes that gap in a different way.

recap.keyIdea: Each transaction reads its own snapshot of row versions, writers lock the rows they change, and a version column lets an application detect that someone else changed a row first.

blocks.text: A snapshot sees the latest version made by a transaction that had committed when it started, so a reader never waits for a writer and sees 100 where an update to 150 is still running. Writers do queue on a row lock, and two that lock rows in opposite order deadlock until one is aborted.
Doing the arithmetic in an atomic `UPDATE`, locking with `FOR UPDATE`, or checking a version column in the `WHERE` clause closes the gap between a read and a write.

lessons.title: Key-value and document stores

lead.text: Many workloads ask the same narrow question over and over: given this id, return this thing, and quickly. A **key-value store** serves it directly. It maps a **key**, a string such as `session:41`, to a **value**, and offers a few operations on a key: set it, get it, delete it, and some arithmetic on it. Redis is the best known, and it keeps its data in memory, which is why it is fast.

What it gives up is everything that needs to look *inside* the data. The relational model can find every customer named Ana or join two tables, and a key-value store can only go to the key. A request for all values that contain "ana" has no shortcut, and it means reading every value, unless the application keeps its own index as more keys.

reveal.text: INCR both changes the stored value and returns the new one, and it works on a number stored as text.

lead.text: The commands are few. `SET key value` stores the text and replies `OK`. `GET key` replies with the value as a string, or `nil` when the key does not exist. `DEL key` removes the key and replies with the number of keys that it removed, 1 or 0. `INCR key` adds 1 to the number stored under the key and replies with the new value as an *integer*, and if the key is missing it starts from 0, so the first `INCR` replies 1.
The figure runs a short session. After `SET a 5`, the command `INCR a` replies 6, and `GET a` then replies the string "6", which is stored as text even though INCR gave an integer.

reveal.text: A missing key is not an error for INCR. It is a counter that has not yet started.
Applications must handle nil, since it is the normal reply for a key that expired or was never set.

lead.text: A value need not be a string. Redis also stores **hashes**, which hold named fields, **lists**, **sets**, and **sorted sets**, in which every member has a score and the set is kept in score order. A sorted set suits a leaderboard: asking for the top ten reads the first ten entries without sorting anything.

Behind this is a different way of designing. A relational design starts from the entities and lets queries be written later, while these stores start from the queries that must be fast and shape the data to answer them. There is also a common misunderstanding about the word NoSQL, which does not mean there is no schema. The schema moves into the application, which decides what each key or field means.

A **document store**, such as MongoDB, keeps a nested record, usually JSON, under a key, and can query the fields inside it. Take an order with three line items. In tables it is a row of `orders` and three rows of `order_items`, and rendering the order page without a join means a read of the order, a read of its items and a read of the customer, which is 3. As one document with the items **embedded**, the same page is a single read.

That is the gain, and it comes from deciding in advance what is read together, which is the access pattern. The cost is that a query for every order that contains ink has to look into each document, and a change to something shared, such as a product name copied into many orders, has to be made in every copy.

reveal.text: The embedded version needs one read, as the order did, which is why document stores are described as fitting data that is read together.

lead.text: The choice for each piece of data is between embedding it in the parent and **referencing** it by its key. Embed it when it is read together with the parent, is small and has a known upper size. A blog post shown with its first five comments is a good example, because nobody asks for the comments alone and there are never more than five. Reference it when it is large, when it can grow without limit, or when many parents share it. A user's profile is shared by thousands of posts, and copying it into each would make one change a thousand edits, so the posts hold a user id instead.

A document that grows without bound is a problem of its own, since every update rewrites a larger document, and the store limits their size. MongoDB documents are limited to 16 mebibytes. A list of followers, or the posts of a busy user, should be referenced, so that each follower or post is a separate document with a link to its parent.

steps.headline: Decide what to embed for blog posts with up to 5 comments each and authors who write many posts.

workedSteps.text: The comments are always shown with the post, there are at most five, and nobody queries them alone. Embed them in the post document.
The author's profile is shared by many posts and changes now and then. Store the author's id in the post and keep the profile in its own document.
A post page has to show the post, its comments and its author.
A change to the profile touches one document, and a new comment adds to one post.

reveal.text: Reference what is large, unbounded or shared, and embed what is small, bounded and read together.

lessons.orientation: Predict the results of simple key-value commands, and choose between embedding and referencing in a document model from the access pattern.
lessons.nextAction: Check a quorum configuration, compute how many keys move when a shard count changes, and choose a store from a workload description.

blocks.text: A page-view counter needs very little from a database. A relational database can do this, with a table, a primary key and an UPDATE, but it also does a good deal that the counter will never use, and some workloads are better served by a store that does only the narrow job and does it in memory.

A **key-value store** is built for that narrow job: it keeps each value under a key and answers by key alone. A document store extends the idea by keeping a nested record under each key, so that data which is read together can be stored together. Both give up the relational database's freedom to search across the data and join it, in return for speed and a simpler layout.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict the replies of simple key-value commands, and decide whether to embed or reference data in a document from the way it is read.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing a store is choosing which queries are fast and which become expensive, and that decision is worth making before the data is there.

recap.keyIdea: Key-value stores answer fast by key and cannot search by value, and in a document store data read together is embedded while data that is large, unbounded or shared is referenced.

blocks.text: INCR on a missing key starts at 0 and replies with an integer, GET replies with a string or nil, and DEL replies with the number of keys it removed. A document with embedded items answers an order page in one read where normalised tables need three.
Embedding suits small, bounded data read with its parent, and referencing suits a profile shared by many posts or a list that can grow without limit.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson covers copies of data across machines, and how to choose a store for a workload.

lessons.title: Replication, sharding and choosing a store

lead.text: A single database server is a limit in three ways: the data must fit on it, every read must be served by it, and if it fails everything stops. **Replication** answers the last two by keeping copies. In the usual layout one node, the **primary**, takes the writes, and sends each change to **replicas**, which serve reads and can take over if the primary fails.

The copies are usually updated *asynchronously*, so a replica may be behind. This **replication lag** gives the read-your-writes problem: a user saves a change, reads it back from a lagging replica, and sees the old data. A replica is also not a backup, since it receives every change, including a mistaken `DELETE`, as faithfully as the good ones.

diagram.alt: A primary database with two replicas. In one view all three hold x equal to 7. In the other the primary and replica 1 hold 7 while replica 2 has not yet received the write and still holds 6.
diagram.caption: A primary and two replicas. Use the buttons to see them in step and then with a lagging replica.

reveal.text: The read must be certain to include at least one replica that has the write, and the rule that makes this so is the quorum condition.

lead.text: Let a write be acknowledged by W of the N replicas, and let a read ask R of them. If the two sets are chosen without any other coordination, they are certain to share a replica exactly when **R + W > N**, and then the read sees at least one replica with the latest write. This is a **quorum** condition, and it is the setting that Amazon's Dynamo paper describes for its replicated store, where N, R and W are chosen for each application.

The figure checks three settings. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2, the sum is 4, which is more than 3, so the sets overlap. With N = 5, W = 3 and R = 2 the sum is 5, which is *not* more than 5, so a read can ask the two replicas that missed the write. Raising R to 3 gives 6, which is more than 5. Overlap guarantees that a replica with the latest write is asked, but the read must still pick the newest of the values it gets back.

diagram.alt: Replica boxes with the replicas that acknowledged the latest write marked on top and the replicas a read asks marked below. With 5 replicas, 3 writes and 2 reads, the two sets can be disjoint. With 5 replicas, 3 writes and 3 reads, they must overlap. With 3 replicas, 2 writes and 2 reads, they must overlap.

reveal.text: The two numbers trade off: a bigger W makes writes slower and allows a smaller R, which makes reads faster.

lead.text: Replication copies the *same* data to several nodes, so it does not help when the data no longer fits on one. **Sharding** splits the data, with each key stored on one shard. The simplest rule is to place key k on node k mod n. When a fourth node is added, the same keys are placed by k mod 4, and the figure shows what happens: only keys 0, 1 and 2 stay where they were, and the other 9 of the 12 move.
Moving data is the expensive part of resizing a cluster, so a rule that changes nearly every placement scales badly.

lead.text: **Consistent hashing** avoids the reshuffle. Imagine the key space 0 to 99 arranged on a ring, with each node at a position on it, and let each key belong to the first node at or after it going clockwise, wrapping round at 99. With nodes at 10, 40 and 70, keys 11 to 40 belong to node 40, keys 41 to 70 to node 70, and keys 71 to 99 and 0 to 10 to node 10.

Now add a node at 60. Only the keys that used to run on past 60 to node 70 and now stop at 60 change owner, which are keys 41 to 60, exactly 20 of the 100. Every other key keeps its owner. The cost of adding a node is therefore only the share of keys it takes over. Consistent hashing was introduced by Karger and colleagues in 1997, and Dynamo's partitioning is based on it.

lead.text: Every store in this course gives something up for something else. A relational database enforces rules, joins freely and offers strong transactions, which suits data with many relationships and rules to keep, such as orders, stock and invoices. When the data is spread over many machines there is a further choice, which the **CAP theorem** states: during a network partition, a replicated store can stay *consistent* and refuse some requests, or stay *available* and risk returning stale data. Eric Brewer put forward the idea in 2000, and Gilbert and Lynch proved a formal version in 2002.

The theorem is often misread as a permanent choice of two out of three, but the choice appears only while a partition is happening. The practical advice is to start with a relational database, which handles most workloads, and to move a part of the system to another kind of store only when a measured need says so.

steps.headline: Choose a store for three workloads.

workedSteps.text: A ledger of accounts and transfers must keep rules and relationships, and needs transactions across rows.
A login session is fetched by its id on every request, expires after a time, and is never searched by content.
A product page shows a product with its few reviews, and is always read as one unit.
All three could live in one relational database, so a different store is chosen only when a measured need, such as speed of lookup, calls for it.

steps.headline: Check the setting N = 7, W = 4, R = 3.

workedSteps.text: The condition for overlap is that R + W is greater than N, where N is 7.
Here W is 4 and R is 3.
The sum of R and W is what the condition compares with N.

reveal.text: Outside a partition a system need not give up either property.

lessons.orientation: Check a quorum configuration, compute how many keys move when a shard count changes, and choose a store from a workload description.
lessons.reviewLabel: Replication, sharding and choosing a store
lessons.nextAction: Design a schema for a business, make it fast, keep it correct under failure, and pick a store for a workload.

blocks.text: A value x is changed from 6 to 7 on the node that takes the writes. The change is sent on to the nodes that hold copies, but it takes time to arrive, so for a moment a read from one of the copies returns 6 while the node that took the write holds 7.

Whether a read is certain to see the newest value comes down to two numbers, how many copies acknowledged the write and how many the read asks, and the sum of the two can be checked against the number of copies. When the data no longer fits on one machine the same kind of counting applies to how many keys move when a machine is added. A choice of store then comes down to which of these costs the workload can afford.

diagram.alt: A primary database with two replicas. In one view all three hold x equal to 7. In the other the primary and replica 1 hold 7 while replica 2 has not yet received the write and still holds 6.
diagram.caption: A primary and two replicas. Use the buttons to see them in step and then with a lagging replica.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to check a quorum setting, count the keys that move when a cluster changes size, and choose a store for a workload.
intro.whyItMatters: A choice of store is a choice of trade-offs, and arithmetic can show what each one costs.

recap.keyIdea: Replicas lag, a quorum needs R + W greater than N, mod sharding moves most keys while consistent hashing moves one arc, and the store should be chosen by the workload.

blocks.text: With 5 replicas, writes to 3 and reads from 2 can miss the latest write, since 5 does not exceed 5, while reads from 3 cannot. Growing from 3 to 4 nodes under key mod n moves 9 of 12 keys, where adding a node to a ring moves only the keys in one arc, 20 of 100 in the example.
Start with a relational database, use a key-value or document store where a measured need calls for it, and remember that the CAP choice only arises during a partition.

questions.prompt: A driving school's description mentions instructors, pupils, driving lessons, a start time, a car registration and an email address. The school records only a bare time for each start, a bare registration for each car and a bare address for each email. Which of these should the model treat as entities?
hints: Ask of each noun whether the school must tell one from another and keep facts about it.
A noun that only supplies a fact about another noun is not a kind of thing.

acceptedIdeas: Instructors, pupils and driving lessons, because each has facts of its own
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Instructors, pupils and driving lessons, because each has facts of its own

questions.onCorrect: Instructors, pupils and driving lessons are identified one by one and have facts of their own. The other three nouns are single values that describe one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: A start time, a car registration and an email address are single values that describe something else. Nothing is kept about them apart from the value, so they are attributes and not kinds of thing.

The school has to tell one driving lesson from another and records a time against each, so a lesson passes the test even though it is an event. An entity is a kind of thing with facts of its own, and it need not be a physical object.

The school keeps only a registration for each car, so there is nothing else to record about a car and the registration is a fact about the lesson. A car would become an entity only if the school began to record facts such as its mileage or its next service.

choices.label: All six, because each is a noun in the description
Instructors and pupils only, because a driving lesson is an event and not a thing
Instructors, pupils, driving lessons and cars, because a car has a registration
Instructors, pupils and driving lessons, because each has facts of its own

questions.prompt: The clinic starts recording the reason for each visit, such as a check-up or a cough. Which entity should have a reason column?
hints: Ask what the reason is a fact about.
If one entity can have several reasons, a single column on that entity cannot hold them.

acceptedIdeas: Appointment, because each visit has its own reason
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Appointment, because each visit has its own reason

questions.onCorrect: The reason changes from visit to visit, so it describes the appointment and goes in the appointment table.

misconceptions.feedback: A patient who comes in once for a check-up and later for a cough has two reasons, and one reason column in the patient row has room for only one.
A doctor sees many patients for many reasons, so one reason column in the doctor row could not hold them all.

choices.label: Appointment, because each visit has its own reason
Doctor, because the doctor writes the reason down
Patient, because the illness belongs to the patient

questions.prompt: The clinic says a doctor sees many patients. Which further question has to be answered before the connection between doctors and patients is fully described?
hints: The statement so far looks along the connection from doctors to patients.
Look along the same connection from the other end.

acceptedIdeas: Whether each patient sees one doctor or may see several
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether each patient sees one doctor or may see several

questions.onCorrect: A connection is described completely only when the question has been asked from both ends: how many patients one doctor sees, and how many doctors one patient sees.

misconceptions.feedback: A doctor seeing many patients is compatible with each patient having one doctor and with each patient having several, and those are different relationships. The other direction has to be asked.
The number of doctors is a fact about the clinic and not about the connection. The connection is described by how many of each side relate to one of the other.

choices.label: Nothing more, because one direction already fixes the connection
Whether each patient sees one doctor or may see several
How many doctors the clinic employs

questions.prompt: Room starts as a column of appointment. The clinic then decides to record each room's capacity and equipment. Why can capacity not stay a column of appointment?
hints: Ask what capacity is a fact about.
Imagine two appointments in the same room.

acceptedIdeas: Capacity is a fact about the room, so every appointment there would repeat it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Capacity is a fact about the room, so every appointment there would repeat it

questions.onCorrect: A fact about the room stored on the appointment would be repeated once per appointment, so it goes in a room table.

choices.label: Capacity is a number, and a column of appointment can only hold dates and times
Capacity is a fact about the doctor who uses the room, so it belongs in the doctor table
Capacity is a fact about the room, so every appointment there would repeat it
Capacity changes between appointments, so a single column cannot keep up with it

misconceptions.feedback: Columns hold numbers without difficulty. The problem is which entity capacity describes.
The capacity is the same whichever doctor uses the room. Ask what the capacity is a fact about.
How often it changes is not the issue. Ask what the capacity is a fact about.

questions.prompt: A smaller clinic has 3 doctors and 12 patients. A table lists which patient has seen which doctor, with at most one row for each patient-doctor pair. What is the largest number of rows it can hold?
hints: Each patient can pair with every doctor.
Count the pairs for one patient, then for all of them.
Multiply the number of patients by the number of doctors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of 12 patients can pair with each of 3 doctors, and 12 × 3 = 36.

questions.onCorrect: With one row for each pair, the table is bounded by 3 × 12 = 36, the size of the many-to-many relationship.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two counts. Each patient can pair with every doctor, so the counts multiply.
That counts patients only. Each patient can appear once for each doctor.

questions.prompt: A library records loans. Each loan is of one book by one member, and a book can be lent many times. What is the cardinality between Book and Loan?
hints: Ask how many loans one book can have, and then how many books one loan can be of.
Compare the two answers: which side can have several partners?

acceptedIdeas: One-to-many
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One-to-many

questions.onCorrect: One book has many loans and each loan is of one book, so the relationship is one-to-many.

misconceptions.feedback: A book can be lent many times, so one book has many loans. One-to-one would allow each book at most one loan.
Each loan is of exactly one book, so a loan has a single book on its side. A relationship is many-to-many only when both sides can have several partners.

choices.label: One-to-one
Many-to-many
One-to-many

questions.prompt: Customer Ana has placed orders 101 and 102, and the `customers` table is given a single column `order_id` to record her orders. What happens when both orders are stored?
hints: Ana is one row of the customers table, and each column of that row holds one value.
Think of a customer with ten orders.

acceptedIdeas: Ana's one row would need two order numbers in a single cell
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ana's one row would need two order numbers in a single cell

questions.onCorrect: A cell holds a single value, so the customer's row has no room for a link to many orders.

misconceptions.feedback: A cell holds one value. Two order numbers in it would be one piece of text, which the database cannot check or search by order.
The link between Ana and her first order would then exist nowhere, so the database could no longer say that order 101 is hers.

choices.label: Ana's one row would need two order numbers in a single cell
Both fit, because a column can hold any number of values
Only the latest order is stored, and the earlier one is left out of the customers table

questions.prompt: `students(id, name)` holds Ana (1), Ben (2), Chloe (3) and Dev (4). `enrollments(student_id, course_id)` holds (1,10), (1,11), (2,10), (3,11), (3,10), (3,12) and (4,12). Which query lists the names of the students who take course 10?
hints: The join condition links a student to their enrollments, and the filter picks the course.
Check which column of `enrollments` holds the course number.

choices.label: `SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE s.id = 10`
`SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = s.id WHERE e.student_id = 10`
`SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id = 10`
`SELECT s.name FROM students s, enrollments e WHERE e.course_id = 10`

acceptedIdeas: `SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id = 10`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id = 10`

questions.onCorrect: The join condition says which enrollments belong to which student, and the `WHERE` clause keeps the rows for course 10, which returns Ana, Ben and Chloe.

misconceptions.feedback: Course 10 is a value in `enrollments.course_id`, and `s.id` is a student number. No student has id 10, so this returns no rows.
This joins a course number to a student number and filters on a student id. No row matches, so it returns nothing.
With no join condition, every student pairs with each course 10 row. It returns 12 rows, each of Ana, Ben, Chloe and Dev three times.

questions.prompt: The seven `enrollments` rows are (1,10), (1,11), (2,10), (3,11), (3,10), (3,12) and (4,12), each written `(student_id, course_id)`. Course 10 is Databases, course 11 is Algorithms and course 12 is Compilers. After the join, how many of the seven rows have the title 'Databases' or 'Algorithms'?
hints: Course 10 is Databases and course 11 is Algorithms.
Count the pairs for each of the two courses.
Add the two counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Course 10 has 3 rows and course 11 has 2, so 3 + 2 = 5 rows remain.

questions.onCorrect: Course 10 has three rows and course 11 has two, so five rows reach the grouping step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows before the filter. The two Compilers rows are removed.
Count the rows for Databases and for Algorithms separately, and add them.

questions.prompt: Now find the students enrolled in both Databases and Compilers: filter to those two titles, group by student, and keep the groups with two distinct titles. How many students does the query return?
hints: Course 12 is Compilers; list who has a row for it.
Which of those students also have a row for course 10?
Count the students that appear in both lists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only Chloe has both: rows (3,10) and (3,12). Ana, Ben and Dev each have just one of the two.

questions.onCorrect: Chloe is the only student with both a Databases row and a Compilers row, so the `HAVING` condition keeps one group.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the groups again. Ana has Databases only, and Dev has Compilers only.
Ben, Ana and Chloe all take Databases, but only one of them also takes Compilers.

questions.prompt: A recipe uses many ingredients, and an ingredient appears in many recipes. Each recipe states an amount of each ingredient it uses. Which table holds the amount column?
hints: Ask whether the amount describes a recipe, an ingredient, or the combination.
Which table has one row for each combination?

acceptedIdeas: `recipe_ingredients`, because the amount describes the pair
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `recipe_ingredients`, because the amount describes the pair

questions.onCorrect: The amount depends on the recipe and the ingredient together, so it is a column of the junction table.

choices.label: Both `recipes` and `ingredients`, so that either side can look it up
`recipe_ingredients`, because the amount describes the pair
`recipes`, because a recipe decides how much of each ingredient to use
`ingredients`, because the amount is a property of the ingredient

misconceptions.feedback: A recipe has many amounts, one for each ingredient, so one column in the recipe row cannot hold them.
An ingredient has a different amount in every recipe that uses it, so one column in the ingredient row cannot hold them.
The amount would be stored twice and could disagree. It describes the pair, so it lives in one place.

questions.prompt: A shop uses its product code as the primary key, and 4 order lines store the code P-100. The supplier renumbers that product to P-150. What has to change to keep the references valid?
hints: The code is copied into every order line that mentions the product.
A copy of a value does not change when the original does.

acceptedIdeas: The product's own row and the 4 order lines that store the code, since each holds a copy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The product's own row and the 4 order lines that store the code, since each holds a copy

questions.onCorrect: The code is the key, so every row that refers to the product holds a copy of it, and all of those copies have to be rewritten together.

misconceptions.feedback: An order line holds its own copy of the code and does not look it up. If only the product row changed, the 4 lines would still say P-100 and would match no product.
Only the lines that store P-100 refer to this product. Lines for other products hold other codes, which have not changed.

choices.label: Every order line in the shop, because the code is shared by the whole table
The product's own row and the 4 order lines that store the code, since each holds a copy
Only the product's own row, because the order lines look the code up when they are read

questions.prompt: A countries table uses each country's two-letter ISO code, such as FR or JP, as its primary key. Is that a natural key or a surrogate key?
hints: Ask where the value comes from: the database, or the world outside it.
FR means France to anyone who reads it, inside the database or not.

acceptedIdeas: A natural key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A natural key

questions.onCorrect: The code comes from the data and means something outside the table, so it can be changed by the body that issues it, as country codes occasionally are.

misconceptions.feedback: A surrogate key is generated by the database and means nothing outside it, while FR is a code the world already uses for France.

choices.label: A surrogate key
A natural key

questions.prompt: A `products` table has `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, `code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE`, `name TEXT NOT NULL` and `price NUMERIC CHECK (price >= 0)`. Which constraint refuses `INSERT INTO products VALUES (6, NULL, 'Glue', 2.00)`?
hints: Look at each value in the row in turn and ask which rule could refuse it.
One value in the row is empty. Which rule refuses an empty value?

acceptedIdeas: `NOT NULL` on `code`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `NOT NULL` on `code`

questions.onCorrect: The `code` column is declared `NOT NULL`, and the statement gives it `NULL`, so the whole row is refused.

misconceptions.feedback: The id 6 is not empty and is not already in use, so the key rule is satisfied.
`UNIQUE` refuses a value that another row already has, and a `NULL` is not a value that equals any other, so the empty code cannot fail this rule.
The price 2.00 is not negative, so the condition `price >= 0` is true for this row.

choices.label: `UNIQUE` on `code`
`PRIMARY KEY` on `id`
`NOT NULL` on `code`
`CHECK` on `price`

questions.prompt: The orders table has three rows: 101 and 102 for Ana, and 103 for Ben. Its foreign key to `customers` is `ON DELETE CASCADE`. What happens to order 103 when Ben's row is deleted from `customers`?
hints: Read the delete action: what does CASCADE do to the rows that refer to the deleted row?
Orders 101 and 102 refer to Ana, so they are not affected.

acceptedIdeas: It is deleted together with Ben's row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is deleted together with Ben's row

questions.onCorrect: CASCADE removes the rows that refer to the deleted row, so order 103 goes with Ben and orders 101 and 102 remain.

misconceptions.feedback: The foreign key forbids an order that refers to a customer who does not exist, so the database cannot leave the order pointing at customer 2.
Refusing the delete is what NO ACTION and RESTRICT do. CASCADE says that the child rows are removed with the parent instead.
Clearing the reference to `NULL` is the `SET NULL` action. `CASCADE` removes the order instead of keeping it.

choices.label: The delete is refused, because an order still refers to Ben
It stays, and its `customer_id` is set to `NULL`
It stays, still holding customer 2, which no longer exists
It is deleted together with Ben's row

questions.prompt: `enrollments(student_id, course_id, grade)` has a key on `(student_id, course_id)` and a foreign key from `student_id` to `students`. `INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (9, 10, 80)` runs when no student 9 exists. Which constraint refuses it?
hints: The pair (9, 10) is not yet in the table, so check the other rule.
Which constraint compares a value with the rows of another table?

acceptedIdeas: The foreign key from `student_id` to `students`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The foreign key from student_id to students

questions.onCorrect: The foreign key requires every `student_id` to match a row of `students`, and there is no student 9.

misconceptions.feedback: The key rule is satisfied by the new pair, but the pair is not the only rule on the table. The foreign key also has to be satisfied, and it is not.
The key refuses a pair that is already stored. The pair (9, 10) is new, so the key is satisfied and something else must refuse the row.

choices.label: The key on `(student_id, course_id)`
No constraint refuses it, because the pair (9, 10) is new
The foreign key from `student_id` to `students`

questions.prompt: Five statements run one after another against `products`, which starts with two rows (P-100 and P-200). Each is accepted or refused on its own. They are: (1) a new row with a fresh id and code, (2) a repeat of id 2, (3) a repeat of code P-100, (4) a price of -1, and (5) a `NULL` code. How many rows does `products` hold at the end?
hints: Check each statement against the rule it might break.
Statements 2 to 5 each break one rule.
Add the accepted rows to the starting two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only statement 1 is accepted: the others break the key, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` rules. 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: A refused statement changes nothing, so only the one row that broke no rule was added.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every statement as accepted. Each of the other four breaks a constraint.
That counts none as accepted. The first statement breaks no rule.

questions.prompt: A `members` table has a `UNIQUE` column `phone`. Two members have no phone number, and both are inserted with `NULL`. In PostgreSQL, what happens to the second insert?
hints: `UNIQUE` refuses a value that another row already has. Ask whether one `NULL` equals another.
`NULL` means unknown.

acceptedIdeas: It is accepted, because two unknown values are not known to be equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is accepted, because two unknown values are not known to be equal

questions.onCorrect: Two unknown values are not known to be equal, so any number of rows can hold `NULL` in a `UNIQUE` column.

misconceptions.feedback: `UNIQUE` refuses a value that another row already has, and `NULL` is not a value that equals another `NULL`. Two unknown values are not known to be the same.
Nothing requires a `UNIQUE` column to be `NOT NULL`. A column that allows `NULL` may hold several of them, which is one of the differences between `UNIQUE` and `PRIMARY KEY`.

choices.label: It is refused, because a UNIQUE column must also be declared NOT NULL
It is accepted, because two unknown values are not known to be equal
It is refused, because both rows have the same value in a UNIQUE column

questions.prompt: `orders_flat` has one row for each product on each order, and every row repeats the name and email of the customer who placed the order. Ana has several order lines and changes her email address. What does keeping the table consistent require?
hints: Ask how many times the table stores Ana's address.
A fact stored in several rows has to be changed in each of them.

acceptedIdeas: Changing each row of Ana's order lines, because each holds a copy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing each row of Ana's order lines, because each holds a copy

questions.onCorrect: Every row for one of Ana's order lines holds a copy of her address, and the table is consistent only when all the copies are changed.

misconceptions.feedback: The table stores the address once for each order line, so there is no single row that holds it. Changing one copy leaves the others with the old address.
Rows for other customers hold other customers' addresses, which have not changed, so they are untouched.

choices.label: Changing one row, because an email address is a single fact
Changing each row of Ana's order lines, because each holds a copy
Changing every row of the table, because the rows depend on one another

questions.prompt: `orders_flat(order_id, customer, email, product, qty)` has four rows: order 1 has two rows for Ana, order 2 has one row for Ben, and order 3 has one row for Ana. Ana's rows all show `ana@old.org`. Someone runs `UPDATE orders_flat SET email = 'ana@new.org' WHERE order_id = 1`. What does `SELECT DISTINCT email FROM orders_flat WHERE customer = 'Ana'` return afterwards?
hints: Count how many of Ana's rows belong to order 1 and how many do not.
Does the table have any rule that makes Ana's rows agree?

choices.label: Two, `ana@new.org` and `ana@old.org`, because order 3 was missed
Only `ana@new.org`, because the update was about Ana
Only `ana@old.org`, because the update was refused as inconsistent
An error, because Ana now has two email addresses

acceptedIdeas: Two, `ana@new.org` and `ana@old.org`, because order 3 was missed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two, `ana@new.org` and `ana@old.org`, because order 3 was missed

questions.onCorrect: The update touched two of Ana's three rows. Nothing in the table ties her rows together, so it now holds two addresses for one person.

misconceptions.feedback: The update changed the rows of order 1 only. Ana's row on order 3 still holds the old address.
The table has no rule linking Ana's rows, so nothing refuses the update.
The table does not know that one customer should have one address. It accepts both.

questions.prompt: A table `enrol_flat` has one row for each student on each course, and every row repeats the course title. Chloe is the only student on Compilers, and when she drops it her row is deleted. The title Compilers vanishes from the table with it. What kind of anomaly is this?
hints: Ask which operation was carried out on the table.
The course title was lost as a side effect of removing something else.

acceptedIdeas: A delete anomaly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A delete anomaly

questions.onCorrect: The course title was stored only beside Chloe's enrolment, so removing the enrolment removed the only record that the course exists.

misconceptions.feedback: An update anomaly is a fact changed in some of its copies and not in others. Here nothing was changed; a fact was lost.
An insert anomaly is a fact that cannot be stored because no row exists to hold it. Here the fact was stored, and then removed by an unrelated delete.

choices.label: A delete anomaly
An update anomaly
An insert anomaly

questions.prompt: A table `loans_flat(loan_id, member_email, book_isbn, book_title, due_date)` has one row for each loan. Each book has exactly one title, and the same book is lent to many members with different due dates. Which column does `book_isbn` determine?
hints: X determines Y when any two rows with the same X always have the same Y.
Take two rows for the same book and ask which columns must agree.

acceptedIdeas: `book_title`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: book_title

questions.onCorrect: Every row for a book shows the same title, because each ISBN is issued to exactly one book.

misconceptions.feedback: The same book is lent many times, so rows with the same ISBN come from different loans and the ISBN does not fix the loan.
The same book is lent to many members, so rows with the same ISBN can have different emails.
Each loan of the book has its own due date, so rows with the same ISBN can have different due dates.

choices.label: `member_email`
`loan_id`
`due_date`
`book_title`

questions.prompt: `orders_flat` has four rows, and their `order_id` values are 1, 1, 2 and 3. Could `order_id` alone be a key of the table?
hints: A key must identify one row, so no value of it may appear on two rows.
Count how many rows each `order_id` has.

choices.label: Yes, because every row has an `order_id` and the column is never empty
No, because order 1 appears on two rows, so `order_id` is not unique
Yes, because `order_id` determines the customer, so it determines every column
No, because a key must have at least two columns

acceptedIdeas: No, because order 1 appears on two rows, so `order_id` is not unique
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because order 1 appears on two rows, so `order_id` is not unique

questions.onCorrect: Two rows share `order_id` 1, so the column cannot identify a row, and the key needs another column added.

misconceptions.feedback: A key must also be unique, and order 1 is repeated, with a different product on each of its rows.
It determines the customer, but not the product, price or quantity of a particular row.
A key can be one column. This one fails because a value repeats.

questions.prompt: A table `enrol_flat(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, grade)` has these dependencies: `student_id` → `student_name`, `course_id` → `course_title`, and `(student_id, course_id)` → `grade`. Which columns form its candidate key?
hints: Follow the dependencies from a starting set of columns and check that all five columns are reached.
A candidate key is minimal: remove any column and it stops determining everything.

acceptedIdeas: `student_id` and `course_id` together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: student_id and course_id together

questions.onCorrect: The pair determines the student's name through `student_id`, the course title through `course_id` and the grade directly, and neither column alone reaches all five.

misconceptions.feedback: `student_id` determines only `student_name`, so the course title and the grade are still not fixed.
`course_id` determines only `course_title`, so the student's name and the grade are still not fixed.
The grade is determined by the pair, so it adds nothing. A candidate key has no unnecessary members, and removing the grade leaves a set that still determines every column.

choices.label: `student_id` and `course_id` together
`student_id`, `course_id` and `grade` together
`student_id` alone
`course_id` alone

questions.prompt: The table (Ana, P1, SQL), (Ben, P1, Rust) is cut into `ep(employee, project)` and `ps(project, skill)`, and the two pieces are joined on `project`. How does the result compare with the original table?
hints: Both rows have the same project, P1, so each piece contains P1 twice.
Ask how many rows of ps match one row of ep when they are joined on project.

acceptedIdeas: It returns the original rows plus extra rows that were never there
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It returns the original rows plus extra rows that were never there

questions.onCorrect: Each of the two rows of ep matches both rows of ps, so the join builds every combination of employee and skill for P1.

misconceptions.feedback: Project P1 appears in both rows of both pieces, so each row of one piece matches both rows of the other, and the join returns more than the original.
No value was deleted by the cut, and a join only combines rows that match. Both pieces contain P1 twice, so every row of one piece finds two partners.

choices.label: It returns the original rows plus extra rows that were never there
It returns exactly the two original rows and nothing more
It returns fewer rows than the original, because the cut lost information

questions.prompt: A different table, (Ana, P1, SQL), (Ben, P2, Rust) and (Cy, P3, SQL), is cut into `ep(employee, project)` and `ps(project, skill)` in the same way, and joining the pieces on `project` returns exactly the three original rows. Why does this split invent nothing?
hints: Count how many times each project appears in ps.
Ask how many rows of ps a single row of ep can match when joined on project.

acceptedIdeas: Each project occurs once in ps, so every row of ep matches exactly one row of ps
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each project occurs once in ps, so every row of ep matches exactly one row of ps

questions.onCorrect: Here project is a key of ps, so each employee meets exactly one skill in the join, which is the test for a lossless split.

misconceptions.feedback: The split of (Ana, P1, SQL) and (Ben, P1, Rust) also kept every value, and its join invented two rows. What matters is how many rows each row matches.
The pieces of the first table shared `project` too, and their join invented two rows. Sharing a column is not enough; it has to be a key of one piece.

choices.label: The cut kept every value, and a join that keeps every value cannot invent rows
Each project occurs once in ps, so every row of ep matches exactly one row of ps
A join always returns the original rows when the pieces share a column

questions.prompt: A table `bookings(flight_no, seat, passenger, departure_time)` has key `(flight_no, seat)`, and `departure_time` depends on `flight_no` alone. Each normal form includes the ones before it. Counting up from 1NF, which is the first normal form the table fails?
hints: Ask whether `departure_time` depends on the whole key or on part of it.
A dependency on part of a composite key is the one the second form removes.

acceptedIdeas: 2NF
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2NF

questions.onCorrect: `departure_time` depends on `flight_no`, which is only part of the key, so it belongs in a `flights` table keyed by `flight_no`.

misconceptions.feedback: Every cell here holds a single value, so the table is in first normal form. The fault is that `departure_time` depends on only part of the key.
Third normal form concerns a non-key column that depends on another non-key column. `flight_no` is part of the key, so this is a dependency on part of a key.

choices.label: 1NF
3NF
2NF

questions.prompt: The flat table stored the Pen's price on each of the two order lines that include a Pen. After the database is normalised to third normal form, how is the Pen's price stored?
hints: In third normal form a fact is stored with the thing it describes.
Ask which table is about products.

acceptedIdeas: Once, in the Pen's row of `products`, and nowhere else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once, in the Pen's row of `products`, and nowhere else

questions.onCorrect: The price is a fact about the product, so it is stored in one cell of products and each order line refers to the product by id.

misconceptions.feedback: The order lines refer to the Pen by its product id, and the price is looked up through it. A copy of the price in `order_items` would bring back the partial dependency that the second step removed.
Order lines that include the Pen hold its id and not its price, so the number of lines that mention it has no effect on how often the price is stored.

choices.label: Still twice, because two order lines include the Pen
Once, in the Pen's row of `products`, and nowhere else
Once in products and once more in each order line for a Pen

questions.prompt: `order_items` has 4 rows and `orders` has 3 rows, and each `order_id` in `order_items` appears in exactly one row of `orders`. Joining `order_items` to `orders` on `order_id` gives how many rows?
hints: Each order line has exactly one matching order.
A one-to-one match keeps the row count the same.
Count the rows in `order_items`.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each `order_items` row matches exactly one `orders` row, so no row is lost or multiplied and the result has 4 rows.

questions.onCorrect: `order_id` is the key of `orders`, so each item finds one order and the row count is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of orders, but every order line joins, and there are four of those.
That would pair every line with every order. The join matches on `order_id` only.

questions.prompt: Using the rebuilt rows, what is Ben's revenue? Ben has one order line, for 4 Pens at a price of 2.
hints: Find Ben's order line.
Multiply quantity by price.
Compare it with the earlier total for the same rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ben's only line is 4 Pens at price 2, so his revenue is 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.onCorrect: The normalised tables reproduce Ben's 8 and Ana's 34, so nothing was lost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity alone. Multiply it by the price of a Pen.
That adds the price and the quantity. Revenue multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A table `courses_flat(student_id, course_id, student_name, grade)` has key `(student_id, course_id)` and the dependency `student_id` → `student_name`. Each normal form includes the ones before it. Counting up from 1NF, which is the first one it fails?
hints: Which part of the key does `student_name` depend on?
Is that the whole key or only part of it?

acceptedIdeas: 2NF
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2NF

questions.onCorrect: `student_name` depends on only part of the key, `student_id`, which is a partial dependency and breaks second normal form.

choices.label: 1NF
None, it is in BCNF
3NF
2NF

misconceptions.feedback: Every cell holds a single value, so first normal form holds.
Third normal form concerns two non-key columns. `student_id` is part of the key, not a non-key column.
A table in BCNF would have no dependency from part of the key. Here one exists.

questions.prompt: Suppose the category were copied into every `fact_sales` row. The Notebook is the only product in the category Stationery and appears in sales 3, 4 and 6. The category is renamed. What would the rename have to change?
hints: Ask how many times the table would store the name Stationery.
Only the sales of products in that category carry the name.

acceptedIdeas: The Notebook's three fact rows, since each holds a copy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Notebook's three fact rows, since each holds a copy

questions.onCorrect: Each sale of the Notebook would hold its own copy of the name, so all three copies have to be changed together.

misconceptions.feedback: With a copy in each fact row, the name is stored once for every sale of the Notebook. Changing one copy leaves the others with the old name.
Rows for the other products carry their own categories, such as Kitchen, which have not been renamed.

choices.label: The Notebook's three fact rows, since each holds a copy
One row, because a category name is a single fact
All six fact rows, because every row has a category column

questions.prompt: `fact_sales` has these rows, written (sale, date, product, units): (1, 1, Mug, 1), (2, 1, Whisk, 2), (3, 2, Notebook, 5), (4, 3, Notebook, 3), (5, 3, Whisk, 2) and (6, 4, Notebook, 2). The Mug and the Whisk are Kitchen products. Dates 1 and 2 are in 2026-11, and dates 3 and 4 are in 2026-12. How many units of Kitchen products were sold in 2026-11?
hints: Find the Kitchen products in `dim_product`.
Keep only their sales on dates in 2026-11.
Add the units, not the amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The Kitchen products are the Mug and the Whisk, and in 2026-11 their sales are 1 and 2, with 1 and 2 units, so 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: This is the revenue report with `SUM(f.units)` in place of `SUM(f.amount)`: the same joins and the same groups, with a different measure added up.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts Kitchen units over both months. Sale 5, a Whisk with 2 units, is on date 3, which is in 2026-12.
That is the revenue for the group, the sum of amount. The question asks for the sum of units.

questions.prompt: An orders table keeps its own copy of each customer's name, taken from customers, so that the list of orders can be shown without a join. What is this practice called? Answer with a single word, such as 'normalising'.
hints: It is the reverse of the process in the previous lesson.
Add the prefix 'de' to the name of that process.

acceptedIdeas: denormalising
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: denormalising

questions.onCorrect: Denormalising trades extra work on every write for cheaper reads, so it needs a reason that has been measured.

misconceptions.feedback: Normalising removes copies. The practice here adds them.

questions.prompt: An orders table could store a total copied from its items. The shop shows order totals 1000 times a day and changes an item on an order 20 times a day. How many times as often is a total read as the source changes?
hints: Compare the two counts.
Divide the number of reads by the number of changes.
Use 1000 and 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1000 reads against 20 changes is 1000 ÷ 20 = 50 times as many reads as changes.

questions.onCorrect: A ratio of reads to changes of 50 means each update of the copy is paid back by many cheaper reads.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of changes. Divide the reads by the changes.
That subtracts the two counts. A ratio divides them.

questions.prompt: A different shop reads order totals 600 times a day and changes items 300 times a day. Is storing a copy of each total worth it?
hints: Each change costs one update of the copy, and each read saves one sum.
How many reads does each change pay for?

choices.label: Yes, because totals are read more often than items change
Yes, because a copy always saves the cost of the sum
Doubtful, because each update saves only two reads
No, because a copy of a total can never be kept right

acceptedIdeas: Doubtful, because each update saves only two reads
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doubtful, because each update saves only two reads

questions.onCorrect: At 600 reads to 300 changes, each update of the copy saves two sums, which is not much for the risk of the copy drifting.

misconceptions.feedback: More reads than changes is necessary, but a ratio of 2 to 1 repays little. The shop in the example read 50 times for each change.
A copy saves the sum on each read and costs an update on each change, so it pays only when reads far outnumber changes.
A copy can be kept right with a trigger or a transaction. The question is whether it pays.

questions.prompt: Product 3, the Whisk, moves from the category Kitchen to the category Home. In the star schema, what has to change to record it?
hints: Ask which table stores the category.
A fact row holds the key of the product, and the key stays the same.

acceptedIdeas: The Whisk's row in `dim_product`, and nothing else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Whisk's row in dim_product, and nothing else

questions.onCorrect: The category is stored once, in the product's dimension row, so one change is enough and every report that joins to it sees the new category.

misconceptions.feedback: The fact rows hold only the Whisk's product key, which has not changed. The category is stored once, in `dim_product`, and the fact rows reach it through the key.
Reports group by category, but the category is not stored in `fact_sales`, so no fact row needs to change.

choices.label: The Whisk's row in `dim_product`, and nothing else
The Whisk's row in `dim_product` and each of its `fact_sales` rows
Every row of `fact_sales`, because reports group by category

questions.prompt: A table of 3,000,000 rows has 60 rows on each page. How many pages does a full scan read?
hints: A full scan reads every page of the table.
The number of pages is the number of rows divided by the rows on each page.
Divide the 3,000,000 rows by the 60 rows on a page.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pages = rows ÷ rows per page = 3,000,000 ÷ 60 = 50,000.

questions.onCorrect: A scan reads every page of the table, so its cost grows in direct proportion to the table size.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. The pages are the rows divided among the pages.
That is the number of rows on one page. Divide the number of rows by it.

questions.prompt: Suppose one page lists 100 other pages, and each of those lists 100 more. Starting from one page and going down two steps, roughly how many pages can you reach in the second step?
hints: The first step reaches 100 pages. Ask how many pages each of those lists.
Each step multiplies the number of pages by the same amount.

acceptedIdeas: About 10,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 10,000

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 100 pages in the first step lists 100 more, so the second step reaches 100 × 100 = 10,000 pages.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two lists instead of multiplying them. Each of the 100 pages in the first step lists 100 pages of its own, so the second step has 100 lists to count, not one.
One more step down would multiply by 100 again, which is a million, but only two steps are taken here.

choices.label: A few hundred
About 10,000

questions.prompt: With a fan-out of 100, how many levels does a B-tree need to index 10,000,000 rows? Take the smallest height h where 100^h is at least the number of rows.
hints: Try the powers of 100 in turn.
Find the first power that reaches 10,000,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100^3 = 1,000,000 is too small and 100^4 = 100,000,000 is enough, so the height is 4.

questions.onCorrect: Each level multiplies the reach by 100, so even tens of millions of rows need only four levels.

misconceptions.feedback: 100^3 is 1,000,000, which is fewer than 10,000,000 rows.
That is the exponent of 10 in the number of rows. Each level multiplies by 100, which is 10 squared.

questions.prompt: A table has 100,000,000 rows (10^8), and the index has fan-out 100. How many levels does the B-tree have?
hints: Try the powers of 100.
Is that enough for the rows?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100^4 = 100,000,000, which is just enough for the rows, so the height is 4.

questions.onCorrect: The tree is exactly full at height 4, only one level more than the 1,000,000-row table needed.

misconceptions.feedback: 100^4 already equals 100,000,000, so a fifth level is not needed.
100^3 is only 1,000,000, far too few for 100,000,000 rows.

questions.prompt: A table has 10,000,000 rows at 50 rows per page, with a B-tree of fan-out 100 and so 4 levels. A lookup reads one page for each level plus one table page. How many times fewer pages does an index lookup read than a full scan?
hints: First find the pages in a scan.
A lookup reads one page for each level plus one more.
Divide the scan pages by the lookup pages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scan reads 10,000,000 ÷ 50 = 200,000 pages and the lookup reads 4 + 1 = 5, so 200,000 ÷ 5 = 40,000.

questions.onCorrect: The ratio grows with the table, because the scan grows in proportion to the rows and the lookup barely grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pages in a scan. Divide it by the pages the lookup reads.
That divides by 4. The lookup also reads the table page, so it reads 5.

questions.prompt: Suppose each row fetched through the index costs 5 sequential page reads' worth of time, and a scan costs 20,000. How many matching rows make the two costs equal, ignoring the tree descent?
hints: The two costs are equal when the cost through the index matches the cost of the scan.
The cost through the index is the cost of one row times the number of rows.
Set 5 times the number of rows equal to 20,000 and solve for the rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal cost means 5 × rows = 20,000, so rows = 20,000 ÷ 5 = 4,000.

questions.onCorrect: A dearer random read moves the break-even to fewer rows, so the index serves a smaller share of the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Equal costs mean 5 times the rows equals 20,000.
That uses a cost of 4 per row. This question uses 5.

questions.prompt: A query matches 30 percent of the rows of a big table. How will the planner most likely read the table?
hints: Compare the cost of 30 percent of the rows, each at several page reads, with the cost of reading every page once.
The break-even in the simple model is about 0.5 percent of the table.

acceptedIdeas: With a table scan, because following the index to that many rows costs more than reading every page once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With a table scan, because following the index to that many rows costs more than reading every page once

questions.onCorrect: Thirty percent is far beyond the break-even, so reading the table in order is cheaper than following the index to every match.

misconceptions.feedback: A lookup is fast for one row, but each row found through the index costs several page reads. Once enough rows match, those reads cost more than the scan.
The break-even is far below half the table, about 0.5 percent in the simple model, because each row found through the index costs several page reads while the scan reads each page once.

choices.label: With an index lookup for each matching row, because an index is always faster than reading the whole table
With a table scan, because following the index to that many rows costs more than reading every page once
With an index lookup for each matching row, because 30 percent is still less than half of the table

questions.prompt: An index on `(last_name, first_name)` lists six entries in order: Shaw Ana, Shaw Ben, Shaw Cy, Smith Ana, Smith Dee, Young Ana. How do the entries with first name Ana sit in the list?
hints: The list is sorted by last name, and only then by first name within each last name.
Find each Ana in the list and look at the entries on either side of it.

acceptedIdeas: Spread out, in separate places among entries with other first names
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Spread out, in separate places among entries with other first names

questions.onCorrect: First names are in order only within a last name, so each Ana sits in its own last-name group, apart from the others.

misconceptions.feedback: The Smiths are together because the list is sorted by last name first. First names are in order only within one last name, so entries with the same first name are not next to each other.
Only one of the three Anas is at the start. The list is sorted by last name first, so Smith Ana and Young Ana come after entries with other first names.

choices.label: Spread out, in separate places among entries with other first names
Together in one run, like the Smiths
Only at the start of the list, because Ana comes first in the alphabet

questions.prompt: An index is declared on `orders(customer_id, order_date)`. Which column must a query filter on for the index to be useful?
hints: Think of the phone book: which of the two columns gives you a place to start reading?
Look at which column the entries are sorted by first.

acceptedIdeas: `customer_id`, because the index is sorted by it first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `customer_id`, because the index is sorted by it first

questions.onCorrect: The entries are ordered by `customer_id` first, so the index can seek on `customer_id`, or on both columns, but not on `order_date` alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The index is sorted by `customer_id` first, and dates are in order only within one customer, so a filter on `order_date` alone has no single place to seek to.
Both columns are stored in the index, but the order of the entries follows `customer_id` first. A filter can seek only on a leading part of that order.

choices.label: `order_date`, because it is the more specific of the two
Either one, because the index contains both columns
`customer_id`, because the index is sorted by it first

questions.prompt: A table of 1,000,000 rows has an index on `country`, a column with 500 equally common values. The query asks for `country = 'NL'`. About how many rows does it match, and is the index worth using?
hints: Rows per value is the table size shared out among the values.
Compare the share matched with the break-even from the previous lesson.

choices.label: About 2,000 rows, 0.2 percent of the table, so the index is worth using
About 500 rows, one for each value, so the index is worth using
About 2,000 rows, but an index never helps on a column with only 500 values
About 2,000 rows, 0.2 percent of the table, so a scan is cheaper than the index

acceptedIdeas: About 2,000 rows, 0.2 percent of the table, so the index is worth using
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 2,000 rows, 0.2 percent of the table, so the index is worth using

questions.onCorrect: Selectivity is the share of rows a condition keeps. At 0.2 percent the index reads a small part of the table, so the planner will use it.

misconceptions.feedback: 500 is the number of distinct values. Each value covers 1,000,000 ÷ 500 = 2,000 rows.
