What matters is the share of rows matched. 2,000 rows is 0.2 percent of the table, well under the break-even.
The break-even in this lesson is around half a percent of the table, and 0.2 percent is below it, so the index wins.

questions.prompt: An index `idx_name` is declared on `emp(last_name, first_name)`. What does the SQLite plan say for `SELECT * FROM emp WHERE last_name = 'L3' AND first_name = 'F3'`?
hints: Apply the leftmost-prefix rule to a filter on both columns.
The brackets name every column the seek uses.

acceptedIdeas: A search on the index using both columns, `(last_name=? AND first_name=?)`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A search on the index using both columns, `(last_name=? AND first_name=?)`

questions.onCorrect: Both columns are a leading part of the index, so the seek uses both and the brackets name both. `SELECT *` still needs the other columns, so the line says `INDEX` and not `COVERING INDEX`.

misconceptions.feedback: `SCAN` is the plan for a filter the index cannot seek on, such as `first_name` alone. Here `last_name` leads, so the index can seek.
Once the seek has reached `last_name` `'L3'`, the first names inside that block are in order too, so the seek uses both columns and the brackets name both.

choices.label: A scan of the whole table, because the index holds two columns
A search on the index using both columns, `(last_name=? AND first_name=?)`
A search on the index that uses only `last_name`, with the rest checked later

questions.prompt: A table of 12,000 employees is spread evenly over 4 departments. About how many rows are in the block of one department?
hints: The departments are equally sized.
Share the table over the departments.
Divide the 12,000 employees among the 4 departments.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12,000 ÷ 4 = 3,000 rows in each department.

questions.onCorrect: An index on (dept, salary) confines the search to one block of 3,000 rows before the salary range is applied.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the numbers. The rows are shared out among the departments.
That is the number of departments. Divide the rows by it.

questions.prompt: A table of 2,000,000 rows has a country column with 250 equally common values. About how many rows match one country?
hints: Equally common values share the table equally.
Divide the rows by the number of values.
Share the 2,000,000 rows over the 250 countries.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2,000,000 ÷ 250 = 8,000 rows for each country.

questions.onCorrect: At 8,000 of 2,000,000 the condition keeps 0.4 percent of the table, which is selective enough for an index.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. The rows are shared among the values.
That is the number of values. Divide the rows by it.

questions.prompt: A table of 1,000,000 orders has an index on `status`. The column holds 'done' for 90 percent of the rows, 'pending' for 6 percent and 'failed' for 4 percent. Using the break-even of about half a percent from this lesson, how is `WHERE status = 'pending'` most likely read?
hints: Work out how many rows 6 percent of the table is.
Compare that share with the break-even.

choices.label: By the index, because 'pending' is the minority value
By a scan, because 60,000 rows is 6 percent of the table
By the index, because the planner always uses an index that exists

acceptedIdeas: By a scan, because 60,000 rows is 6 percent of the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By a scan, because 60,000 rows is 6 percent of the table

questions.onCorrect: Even the rarer values of this column match more than the break-even share, so an index on `status` alone would rarely be chosen.

misconceptions.feedback: A minority value can still be a large share. 6 percent is far above the break-even.
The planner compares costs, and following the index to 60,000 rows costs more than reading each page once.

questions.prompt: Table R has 200 rows and table S has 3,000 rows, with no index on either. A naive nested-loop join checks every pair of rows. Roughly how many pair comparisons is that?
hints: For one row of R, the loop checks every row of S.
The loop repeats that for every row of R.

acceptedIdeas: About 600,000, one for each pair of rows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 600,000, one for each pair of rows

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 200 rows of R is checked against all 3,000 rows of S, so the work is the product of the two sizes, 600,000 comparisons.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes, which is the work of a hash join. A nested loop checks the whole of S for every row of R, so the two sizes are multiplied.
One pass over S would find matches for a single row of R. The loop has to make that pass again for each of the 200 rows.

choices.label: About 600,000, one for each pair of rows
About 3,200, one for each row of either table
About 3,000, one pass over the larger table

questions.prompt: R has 200 rows and S has 3,000 rows, with no index on either. A naive nested loop makes about 600,000 pair comparisons. Why does a hash join over the same tables make only about 3,200 operations?
hints: A hash lookup finds the matching rows of R without comparing against all 200.
Build touches each row of R once and probe touches each row of S once.

choices.label: It compares every pair, but each comparison is cheaper
It builds a table of R and probes it with S
It reads only the 200 rows of R and ignores S
It sorts both tables, so each row needs one comparison

acceptedIdeas: It builds a table of R and probes it with S
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It builds a table of R and probes it with S

questions.onCorrect: Build handles 200 rows and probe handles 3,000, so 3,200 operations in place of 600,000 pair comparisons, and the gap widens as the tables grow.

misconceptions.feedback: The saving is in the number of operations. A hash join does not look at every pair.
Every row of S is probed against the hash table, so S is read once in full.
That describes a merge join. A hash join needs no sort.

questions.prompt: In another plan, the scan of customers was estimated at 5,000 rows and returned 4,800, while the scan of payments was estimated at 50 rows and returned 60,000. The join and the sort above them were planned for the estimated sizes. Where did the plan first go wrong?
hints: Compare the estimate and the actual count for each scan.
Steps above a wrong estimate inherit its mistake, so look for the lowest step that is wrong.

acceptedIdeas: At the scan of payments, because its estimate was far too low
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the scan of payments, because its estimate was far too low

questions.onCorrect: The scan of payments returned 1,200 times more rows than estimated, and the join and sort above it were planned for a size that did not occur.

misconceptions.feedback: The estimate for `customers` was within a few percent of what the scan returned, so nothing went wrong there. The size of an estimate does not matter; the gap between estimate and actual count does.
The sort inherited its size from the steps below it. A plan is read from the leaves, and the first step whose estimate is wrong is the one to blame.

choices.label: At the scan of customers, because 5,000 is the larger estimate
At the sort at the top, because it is the last step
At the scan of payments, because its estimate was far too low

questions.prompt: An indexed nested loop seeks in a 3-level index on the inner table for each outer row. How many pages does one seek read, counting the table page that holds the row?
hints: An index seek reads one page for each level of the tree.
The row itself is then fetched from the table.
Add the table page to the index levels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The seek reads 3 index pages and then 1 table page, so 4 pages.

questions.onCorrect: Each seek costs the height of the tree plus one table page, as in the earlier lesson on indexes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the index levels. The row itself is in a table page.
That is only the table page. The seek has to descend the tree first.

questions.prompt: Now R has 2,000 rows and the same 3-level index is on S. How many page reads does the indexed nested loop make in total?
hints: Each iteration of the loop seeks once in the index.
A seek reads the index levels and then one table page.
Multiply the number of outer rows by the pages one seek reads.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 2,000 outer rows reads 4 pages, so 2,000 × 4 = 8,000.

questions.onCorrect: The cost grows in step with the number of outer rows, and the seek cost barely changes with the size of S.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one read for each outer row. Each seek reads 4 pages.
That counts 3 pages for each seek. The table page makes 4.

questions.prompt: A filter leaves 10 rows from table R. Table S has 5,000,000 rows and an index on the join column. Which strategy is likely to be cheapest?
hints: How many seeks does the outer side need?
What would the other strategies read?

acceptedIdeas: Nested loop with seeks in the index on S
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nested loop with seeks in the index on S

questions.onCorrect: Ten seeks of about 4 pages each cost about 40 page reads, against millions of rows for the strategies that read all of S.

choices.label: Nested loop with seeks in the index on S
Hash join over both tables
A nested loop with no index
Merge join after sorting both tables

misconceptions.feedback: A hash join would read all 5,000,000 rows of S, to serve only 10 outer rows.
Sorting both tables means reading all of S first. Ten seeks are far cheaper.
Without an index each of the 10 rows would be checked against 5,000,000 rows.

questions.prompt: A is 800 and B is 300. A transfer of 200 runs as two separate statements in autocommit mode, where each statement is saved as soon as it finishes, a debit of A and then a credit to B, and the server crashes between them. What is the total of A and B afterwards?
hints: In autocommit mode each statement commits as soon as it finishes.
The debit runs first, and the crash comes before the credit.

acceptedIdeas: 900, because the debit was kept and the credit never happened
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 900, because the debit was kept and the credit never happened

questions.onCorrect: The debit committed on its own, so A is 600 and B is still 300. The 200 has left the system and the database cannot tell that a credit was missing.

misconceptions.feedback: In autocommit mode the debit is already a transaction of its own and has committed. The database has no record that a credit was meant to follow, so it cannot complete the transfer.
The debit runs first, so it is the statement that has finished when the crash comes. The credit has not run, so it cannot be the one that was kept.

choices.label: 1,100, the same as before, because the database completes the transfer when it restarts
1,300, because the credit was kept and the debit never happened
900, because the debit was kept and the credit never happened

questions.prompt: A is 800 and B is 300. A transaction debits A by 200 and credits B by 200. The server crashes after both updates but before COMMIT. What are A and B after recovery?
hints: Changes in a transaction take effect when COMMIT succeeds, and not before.
Ask whether a commit record for this transaction can be in the log.

acceptedIdeas: A is 800 and B is 300, because the transaction never committed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is 800 and B is 300, because the transaction never committed

questions.onCorrect: Without a commit the transaction is undone as a whole, so both balances return to what they were before it began.

misconceptions.feedback: Completed updates are not enough. Their changes take effect only when COMMIT succeeds, and the crash came first.
Inside a transaction no statement takes effect on its own, so the debit is not saved separately from the credit. Recovery undoes the whole transaction.

choices.label: A is 600 and B is 500, because both updates were completed
A is 600 and B is 300, because the debit was saved before the credit
A is 800 and B is 300, because the transaction never committed

questions.prompt: A bank's server confirms a deposit when COMMIT returns, and a second later it loses power. When it restarts, the deposit is still there. Which ACID property guarantees that? Answer with the property's name.
hints: The deposit had already committed when the power failed.
Ask which of the four letters is about committed work surviving a crash.

acceptedIdeas: durability
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: durability

questions.onCorrect: Durability is the guarantee about committed work. Atomicity is about uncommitted work, which vanishes.

misconceptions.feedback: Atomicity concerns a transaction that did not commit. This question is about one that did.

questions.prompt: A is 700 and B is 150. A transfer of 150 commits, and the commit record reaches the log on disk, but the server crashes before any table page is written. What does recovery produce?
hints: Durability comes from the commit record in the log and not from the table pages.
After a crash the database reads the log and replays the transactions whose commit record is present.

acceptedIdeas: A is 550 and B is 300, because recovery replays the committed transfer from the log
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is 550 and B is 300, because recovery replays the committed transfer from the log

questions.onCorrect: The commit record is in the log, so recovery replays the whole transfer and the balances come out at 550 and 300.

misconceptions.feedback: Committing means that the log record is durable, not that the table files were written. The log is what recovery reads, so the unwritten pages do not decide the outcome.
The debit and the credit belong to one transaction, and its commit record covers both, so recovery replays them together or not at all.

choices.label: A is 550 and B is 150, because the debit was replayed and the credit was lost
A is 550 and B is 300, because recovery replays the committed transfer from the log
A is 700 and B is 150, because the table pages were never written

questions.prompt: A is 900 and B is 100. A transfer of 250 commits, and its commit record is in the log, but the server crashes before any table page is written. What is A after recovery?
hints: Recovery replays the committed change from the log.
The debit lowers A by the amount of the transfer.
Subtract the transfer from A's starting balance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Recovery replays the committed debit, so A = 900 − 250 = 650.

questions.onCorrect: The committed debit is applied by recovery, which restores A to 650 and B to 350.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value on the page before recovery. The committed debit is replayed.
That adds the amount. A is the account being debited.

questions.prompt: The `accounts` table has `CHECK (balance >= 0)`. A is 50, and a transaction debits A by 100 and credits B by 100. The debit breaks the `CHECK`, so the statement fails and the transaction is rolled back. What is the state afterwards?
hints: A CHECK refuses a row that breaks its condition.
A transaction takes effect together or not at all.

acceptedIdeas: A is 50 and B is unchanged, because the whole transaction is rolled back
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A is 50 and B is unchanged, because the whole transaction is rolled back

questions.onCorrect: The transaction is undone as a whole, so A keeps 50 and B receives nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: The two statements are one transaction, and it is rolled back as a whole. The credit does not run as a separate statement once the transaction has failed.
A CHECK constraint refuses a row for which the condition is false, so a balance of -50 is never stored.

choices.label: A is 50 and B is unchanged, because the whole transaction is rolled back
A is 50 and B is 100 higher, because the credit is a separate statement that can still run
A is -50 and B is 100 higher, because a CHECK only reports a warning

questions.prompt: x = 40. T1 and T2 both read x. Then T1 writes x + 10 and commits, and T2 writes x + 30, each using the value it read. What is x finally?
hints: T2 uses the value it read, before T1 wrote anything.
The later write replaces whatever is in the row.

acceptedIdeas: 70, because T2 writes a value built from the 40 it read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 70, because T2 writes a value built from the 40 it read

questions.onCorrect: T2 added 30 to the 40 it had read, so it wrote 70 and T1's change of 10 was overwritten.

misconceptions.feedback: Both additions would be applied only if T2 had started from T1's result. T2 computed its value from the 40 it read, before T1 wrote anything.
T2 writes after T1 commits, and its write replaces the value in the row. Commit order does not protect T1's result from a later write.

choices.label: 70, because T2 writes a value built from the 40 it read
50, because T1 committed first and its value is kept
80, because both additions are applied to the same value

questions.prompt: x = 50. One transaction adds 5 and another adds 20, each reading x and writing the sum. If they run one after the other, in either order, what can x finally be?
hints: When one transaction finishes before the other starts, what value does the second one read?
Compare with the schedule in which both read 50.

choices.label: Only 75, because the second addition builds on the first
75 or 70, depending on which runs first
55 or 70, because the later transaction replaces the earlier one
75 or 55 or 70, because the order decides which one wins

acceptedIdeas: Only 75, because the second addition builds on the first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only 75, because the second addition builds on the first

questions.onCorrect: Serial runs always give 75. The anomalies in this lesson are overlapping schedules whose result no serial run could produce.

misconceptions.feedback: Addition gives the same total in either order. The second transaction reads the value the first one wrote.
A later write replaces an earlier one only when it was built from a stale value. When they run one after the other, it was not.
Winning only matters when the transactions overlap. Run one after the other, nothing is overwritten.

questions.prompt: T1 reads the price of product 7 and gets 4.00. T2 changes that price to 4.50 and commits. T1 reads product 7 again and gets 4.50. What is this anomaly called?
hints: T2 had committed its change before T1 read the row again.
The same row was read twice and gave two different values.

acceptedIdeas: A non-repeatable read, because one row changed between reads
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A non-repeatable read, because one row changed between reads

questions.onCorrect: T1 read the same row twice and got different prices because T2 committed in between, which is a non-repeatable read.

misconceptions.feedback: A dirty read uses a change that has not been committed. T2's change was committed before T1 read it a second time.
A phantom read concerns a set of rows, with a new row appearing between two queries. Here the same row has a different value.
A lost update is a write that overwrites another. T1 only reads in this schedule.

choices.label: A non-repeatable read, because one row changed between reads
A dirty read, because T1 saw a change that T2 had not committed
A lost update, because T2's write replaced a write of T1
A phantom read, because a new row appeared between two queries

questions.prompt: A rule says at least 2 of 4 doctors must stay on call. Three doctors each check that the count is 4, which is more than 2, and each takes themselves off call as a separate transaction at Repeatable Read, all at the same time. Which describes the outcome?
hints: Each transaction works from a snapshot in which the count is 4.
Repeatable Read does not stop two transactions from updating different rows.

acceptedIdeas: One doctor stays and the rule is broken, since each changed a different row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One doctor stays and the rule is broken, since each changed a different row

questions.onCorrect: Each transaction was right for the data it saw, but together they took three doctors off call and left one, which is write skew.

misconceptions.feedback: The three transactions update different rows, so none of them waits for another and none is refused. Repeatable Read does not look at the rule between the rows.
Reading the same data does not cause an abort. Repeatable Read aborts a transaction only when it tries to update a row that has changed since its snapshot, and these updates touch different rows.

choices.label: One doctor stays and the rule is broken, since each changed a different row
Two doctors stay on call, because the database refuses the third change
All three transactions are aborted, because they read the same data

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL transaction starts with a plain BEGIN, naming no isolation level. It reads a row twice, and the second read shows a change that another transaction committed in between. Which isolation level is it running at?
hints: A BEGIN that names no level uses the default.
Only one of the three levels lets a later statement see data committed after the transaction began.

acceptedIdeas: Read Committed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Read Committed

questions.onCorrect: Read Committed is the default, and since each statement sees what was committed when it began, it allows exactly this non-repeatable read.

misconceptions.feedback: Serializable gives the whole transaction one snapshot, so the second read could not see the change. It also has to be requested, and this BEGIN named no level.
Repeatable Read gives the whole transaction one snapshot, so the second read would show the old value. It also has to be requested, and this BEGIN named no level.

questions.prompt: A Serializable transaction is aborted with a serialisation failure. What should the application do?
hints: The failure says nothing is wrong with the transaction itself.
Ask what the transaction conflicted with, and whether that is still the case.

acceptedIdeas: Run the whole transaction again from the start
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Run the whole transaction again from the start

questions.onCorrect: A serialisation failure means the transaction conflicted with another, and running it again against the new data normally succeeds.

misconceptions.feedback: A lower level would let write skew back in. The failure is the price of the protection, and not a fault to switch off.
An aborted transaction's changes were not applied, so ignoring the error loses them.

choices.label: Lower the isolation level so that the error stops happening
Ignore the error, because the transaction's changes were saved
Run the whole transaction again from the start

questions.prompt: x = 100. T1 adds 10 and T2 adds 25, overlapping as in the lost update, at Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL. T1 commits first. T2's write is refused because x changed, and T2 retries from the start and succeeds. What is x finally?
hints: What does the retried transaction read?
The refused attempt left nothing behind.

choices.label: 125, because T2 still uses the 100 it first read
110, because T2's change is discarded after the refusal
135, because the retry reads 110 and adds 25
Either 110 or 125, depending on the timing of the retry

acceptedIdeas: 135, because the retry reads 110 and adds 25
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 135, because the retry reads 110 and adds 25

questions.onCorrect: The retry sees T1's change, so the result equals a serial run and the lost update has been turned into an error the application handles.

misconceptions.feedback: The retry begins again and reads the value T1 committed, which is 110.
T2 is refused once and then runs again, so its addition is applied.
A retry always reads the committed state, so the result is the serial one.

questions.prompt: A row holds 200 in a version created by transaction 5 (tx 5) and ended by tx 8, and holds 260 in a version created by tx 8. A reader's snapshot was taken while tx 8 was still running. What does the reader see?
hints: A snapshot records which transactions had committed when it was taken.
Ask whether tx 8 had committed at that moment.

acceptedIdeas: 200, because that version was the current one at the snapshot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 200, because that version was the current one at the snapshot

questions.onCorrect: Tx 8 was still running, so its new version is invisible to this snapshot and the reader sees 200 without waiting.

misconceptions.feedback: Tx 8 had not committed when the snapshot was taken, so the version it created does not count for this reader.
A plain `SELECT` takes no row lock, so it never waits for a writer. It reads the version that was visible to its snapshot.

choices.label: 260, because it is the newest version of the row
200, because that version was the current one at the snapshot
Nothing yet, because the reader must wait for tx 8 to finish

questions.prompt: The same row holds 200 in a version created by tx 5 and ended by tx 8, and 260 in a version created by tx 8. A new reader takes its snapshot after tx 8 has committed. What does it see?
hints: The snapshot sees the latest version created by a transaction that had committed.
Ask which transaction created each version and whether it had committed.

acceptedIdeas: 260, because tx 8 had committed when the snapshot was taken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 260, because tx 8 had committed when the snapshot was taken

questions.onCorrect: Tx 8 had committed, so the version it created is the latest visible one and the earlier version has ended for this reader.

misconceptions.feedback: The first version was ended by tx 8, and tx 8 had committed, so that version is no longer the latest one this snapshot can see.
Tx 8 has already committed, so there is nothing to wait for. Even while a writer is running, a plain `SELECT` never waits.

choices.label: 260, because tx 8 had committed when the snapshot was taken
It waits for tx 8, because the row was changed recently
200, because that version was created first

questions.prompt: T1 updates account 3 and then account 9. T2 updates account 9 and then account 3, and when the two run together they sometimes deadlock. What change to T2 removes the deadlock?
hints: A deadlock needs each transaction to hold the row that the other wants next.
If both ask for account 3 first, the second one waits.

acceptedIdeas: Update account 3 first and then account 9, the same order as T1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Update account 3 first and then account 9, the same order as T1

questions.onCorrect: With the same order, whichever transaction locks account 3 first also gets account 9, so the other simply waits and no cycle can form.

misconceptions.feedback: Starting on different rows is exactly what makes the cycle: each transaction then holds the row the other wants next.
The isolation level does not remove the cycle. Two writers that wait for each other's row locks deadlock at Read Committed as well.

choices.label: Update account 3 first and then account 9, the same order as T1
Run T2 at Read Committed, which never deadlocks
Keep its order, so that T1 and T2 never start on the same row

questions.prompt: x = 200. Two transactions run at the same time at Read Committed: `UPDATE t SET x = x + 15` and `UPDATE t SET x = x + 40`. The second waits for the row lock, then re-evaluates. What is x finally?
hints: The second update waits for the first to commit.
After waiting, it re-evaluates `x + 40` on the committed row and not on the 200 it started from.
Add both increments to the starting value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second update waits for the first to commit, then adds 40 to the new value 215: 200 + 15 + 40 = 255.

questions.onCorrect: Taking the lock before reading the value removes the gap that caused the lost update.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the lost-update result, which needs a separate read in the application. Here the arithmetic happens in the database, after the lock.
That keeps only the first update. The second waits, then applies its +40.

questions.prompt: The row with id 12 now has version 9. You run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 90, version = 9 WHERE id = 12 AND version = 8`. What does the database report?
hints: The `WHERE` clause has two conditions, one on the id and one on the version.
Ask which rows match both conditions.

acceptedIdeas: 0 rows updated, because no row has both id 12 and version 8
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0 rows updated, because no row has both id 12 and version 8

questions.onCorrect: No row has both id 12 and version 8, so nothing is updated, and the count of 0 tells the application that someone else changed the row.

misconceptions.feedback: The `WHERE` clause needs both conditions to be true, and the version of the row is 9. The row exists, but it does not match.
The statement is valid and raises no error. A `WHERE` clause that matches nothing updates nothing, and the count of rows is how the application finds out.

choices.label: An error, because the version in the row does not match
1 row updated, because the row with id 12 exists
0 rows updated, because no row has both id 12 and version 8

questions.prompt: Two users read account 7 at balance 100 and version 3. User 1 runs `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 150, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3`, and it updates 1 row. What version does the row have afterwards?
hints: Read the `SET` clause for what happens to `version`.
The `WHERE` clause only decides whether the row is matched.

choices.label: 4, because the update added one to the version
3, because the version changes only when a row is read
1, the number of rows updated

acceptedIdeas: 4, because the update added one to the version
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4, because the update added one to the version

questions.onCorrect: Version 4 is what user 2's `WHERE version = 3` will no longer match, which is how the conflict is found.

misconceptions.feedback: The version is a column that the update itself writes. Reading leaves it alone.
The count of rows updated is what the database reports. The version is a value in the row.

questions.prompt: User 2 wanted to add 30 to the balance. After user 1's save, the row is at balance 150 and version 4. User 2 re-reads, adds 30 and saves with `WHERE version = 4`. What is the balance afterwards?
hints: The retry starts from the re-read balance.
What is that balance?
Add 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The retry applies the +30 to the new balance, so 150 + 30 = 180, and the version becomes 5.

questions.onCorrect: The retry builds on the latest data, so both users' changes are kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is user 2's first attempt, 100 + 30, which was refused. The retry starts from 150.
That is user 1's balance. User 2's retry adds 30 to it.

questions.prompt: Two transactions each select the last free seat and then update it, and both succeed at Read Committed. Which clause added to the `SELECT` makes the second one wait for the first? Give the two-word clause.
hints: The clause locks the rows as they are read.
It is written after the `WHERE` clause of the `SELECT`.

acceptedIdeas: FOR UPDATE
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: FOR UPDATE

questions.onCorrect: FOR UPDATE takes the row lock at the read, so the second transaction waits and then sees the seat as taken.

misconceptions.feedback: A shared lock does not stop another transaction from also reading and then updating, so both could still proceed.

questions.prompt: On a new store, `SET n 10` runs, and then `INCR n`, which adds one to the number stored under `n`, runs twice. What does the second `INCR` return?
hints: SET n 10 stores the number 10 under the key.
Each INCR adds 1 to the stored number and replies with the result.

acceptedIdeas: 12, the number stored after two increments
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 12, the number stored after two increments

questions.onCorrect: The first INCR makes the stored number 11, and the second makes it 12 and replies with that new value.

misconceptions.feedback: INCR does not count its own calls. It adds 1 to the number stored under the key, which SET had already made 10.
INCR replies with the new value, after the addition. The first INCR replies 11, and the second adds one more to that.

choices.label: 12, the number stored after two increments
2, the number of times INCR has run
11, the value before the second increment

questions.prompt: On an empty store: `SET a 5`, then `INCR a`, then `INCR a`, then `DEL a`, then `INCR a`. What does the last `INCR` reply?
hints: What does `DEL` do to the value stored under the key?
How does `INCR` treat a key that does not exist?

choices.label: 8, because the counter keeps its history after `DEL`
1, because `INCR` starts a deleted key at 0
0, because a missing key has nothing to add to
An error, because the key no longer exists

acceptedIdeas: 1, because `INCR` starts a deleted key at 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1, because `INCR` starts a deleted key at 0

questions.onCorrect: The key was removed, so the next `INCR` creates it at 0 and raises it to 1.

misconceptions.feedback: `DEL` removes the key and its value. Nothing of the earlier 5, 6 and 7 is kept.
`INCR` treats a missing key as 0 and adds one, so it replies 1.
A missing key is not an error for `INCR`. It is a counter that has not started.

questions.prompt: On an empty store, `SET b 7` runs, and then `GET c`. What does `GET c` reply? Answer with the reply as Redis writes it.
hints: Ask whether the key c was ever set.
For a missing key the reply is not an empty string and not an error.

acceptedIdeas: nil
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: nil

questions.onCorrect: Only b was set, so c does not exist, and a missing key and an empty string are different things, so GET replies nil.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is stored under b. GET looks up only the key it is given, and nothing was stored under c.
Zero is a possible stored value, and INCR works with it. A missing key replies with no value at all.

questions.prompt: A product page shows a product, its 4 photos and the name of its category. In three normalised tables, and without a join, the page takes a separate read for each table. What would let the page be answered with a single read?
hints: The page needs data from three places, and each place costs a read.
A single read can return only what is stored together.

acceptedIdeas: Storing the product as one document with its photos and category embedded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Storing the product as one document with its photos and category embedded

questions.onCorrect: Data that is read together is stored together, so one read returns the product with everything the page shows.

misconceptions.feedback: An index makes one read of the photos faster, but the product, the photos and the category would still be three separate reads.
Three keys are still three reads. Moving the tables into a different kind of store does not put the data that is read together in one place.

choices.label: Storing the product as one document with its photos and category embedded
Storing each of the three tables under its own key in a key-value store
Adding an index on the photos table so that its rows are found faster

questions.prompt: A blog post document embeds its comments and holds only the id of its author, whose profile is a separate document. How many reads does a post page need?
hints: Which parts of the page are inside the post document?
A reference needs a second read to follow.

choices.label: One, because the post document holds everything the page shows
Two, one for the post with its comments and one for the author
Six, one for the post, one for each of up to five comments, and one for the author

acceptedIdeas: Two, one for the post with its comments and one for the author
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two, one for the post with its comments and one for the author

questions.onCorrect: Embedding the comments saves a read for each one, and referencing the author keeps one profile shared by all of that author's posts.

misconceptions.feedback: The comments are embedded, but the author's profile is a separate document found by its id.
The comments are embedded in the post, so reading the post returns them.

questions.prompt: A key-value store holds 1,000,000 keys and has no index apart from the keys. You need every value that contains the text ana. How many values must the store read to be sure of finding them all?
hints: A match could be under any key.
Ask what the store has to start from when no key is given.

acceptedIdeas: Every one of the 1,000,000 values, because a match could be under any key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every one of the 1,000,000 values, because a match could be under any key

questions.onCorrect: A store organised only by key has no way to find a value by its content, which is the trade it makes for speed.

misconceptions.feedback: A key says nothing reliable about the text inside its value. The match is in the value, and it could be under any key.
The store keeps no index on the contents. Without one, nothing narrows the search.

choices.label: Only the values whose keys contain ana, because the key points to the value
Every one of the 1,000,000 values, because a match could be under any key
A small sample, because the store keeps a hidden index on the contents

questions.prompt: A store keeps N = 3 copies of each value, and each write is acknowledged by W = 2 of them. What is the smallest number of copies a read can ask and still be certain that at least one of them has the latest write?
hints: Ask how many copies could have missed the write.
A read of that many copies could land entirely on the ones that missed it, so it needs at least one more.

acceptedIdeas: Two, so that at least one copy asked has the write
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two, so that at least one copy asked has the write

questions.onCorrect: Only one of the three copies lacks the write, so a read of two copies has to include at least one that holds it.

misconceptions.feedback: The one copy that missed the write could be the one asked. Two acknowledged the write, but the read has no way of choosing which copies those were.
Only one copy missed the write, so a read of two copies must include at least one that has it. Asking all three would also work, but it is more than the guarantee needs.

choices.label: One, because two of the three copies have the write
Two, so that at least one copy asked has the write
Three, because anything fewer could miss the write

questions.prompt: A store has N = 5 replicas and each write is acknowledged by W = 4. What is the smallest R that guarantees a read overlaps the latest write?
hints: The condition is R + W greater than N.
Try R = 1 first, and see whether 1 + 4 exceeds 5.

choices.label: 1, because 4 of the 5 replicas already hold the write
3, because a read must reach a majority of the replicas
2, because R + 4 must exceed 5
4, because R must equal W

acceptedIdeas: 2, because R + 4 must exceed 5
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2, because R + 4 must exceed 5

questions.onCorrect: The two numbers trade off: raising W lets R be smaller, which makes reads cheaper at the cost of slower writes.

misconceptions.feedback: One replica could be the one without the write. R + W must exceed N, and 1 + 4 does not exceed 5.
A majority is enough with some settings, but the rule is R + W > N. With W = 4, two replicas already make the sum 6.
R and W do not have to be equal. Only their sum has to exceed N.

questions.prompt: Keys 0 to 11 are placed by key mod 3. The cluster grows to 6 nodes and keys are placed by key mod 6. How many of the 12 keys change node?
hints: Compare each key's old node with its new node.
Work out k mod 3 and k mod 6 for each key, starting from 0.
Count the keys whose node changes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A key stays only if k mod 3 equals k mod 6, which holds for 0, 1, 2, 6, 7 and 8. The other 6 keys move.

questions.onCorrect: Doubling the node count keeps half of the keys in place with this rule, which is better than the 3 to 4 case but still moves many.

misconceptions.feedback: Some keys land on the same node under both rules. Compare k mod 3 with k mod 6 for each.
That counts only keys 0, 1 and 2 as staying. Check the larger keys too.

questions.prompt: On the ring of keys 0 to 99 with nodes at 10, 40 and 70, a node is added at 25. Each key belongs to the first node at or after it, going clockwise. How many keys change owner?
hints: Which keys fall between the node before 25 and 25 itself?
The previous node is at 10.
Count the keys from 11 to 25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Keys 11 to 25 used to belong to node 40 and now stop at the new node 25, which is 25 − 10 = 15 keys.

questions.onCorrect: Only the arc between the new node and the one before it moves, and nothing else is disturbed.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the whole arc from 10 to 40. Only the part up to the new node changes.
That is the position of the new node. Count the keys between node 10 and the new node.

questions.prompt: A bank ledger needs strict rules, many relationships and safe transfers between accounts. Which kind of store fits?
hints: Ask which kind of store enforces rules and offers transactions across rows.
A transfer changes two accounts at once.

acceptedIdeas: A relational database, because it enforces rules and keeps transfers atomic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A relational database, because it enforces rules and keeps transfers atomic

questions.onCorrect: A ledger has many relationships and rules to keep, and transfers need transactions across rows, which a relational database provides.

misconceptions.feedback: A key-value store answers quickly by key, but it can neither enforce rules between values nor join them, and a transfer needs both accounts to change together.
A document store keeps data that is read together in one record. A transfer changes two accounts, and the rules and relationships of a ledger are better enforced by the database itself.

choices.label: A key-value store, because lookups by key are the fastest of any store
A relational database, because it enforces rules and keeps transfers atomic
A document store, because each account can be kept as one nested record

questions.prompt: N = 7 replicas, writes acknowledged by W = 4 and reads from R = 3. Does every read overlap the latest write?
hints: The overlap condition is R + W greater than N.
Add R and W and compare with N.

choices.label: No, since R + W = 7 does not exceed N
Yes, because R + W = 7 equals N
Yes, because W = 4 is a majority of 7
No, because R must be a majority of N

acceptedIdeas: No, since R + W = 7 does not exceed N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since R + W = 7 does not exceed N

questions.onCorrect: With a sum of 7 a read can pick the 3 replicas that missed the write. R = 4 would make the sum 8 and close the gap.

misconceptions.feedback: The sum must exceed N. At exactly N, 3 replicas can be chosen from the 3 that lack the write.
A majority write alone does not guarantee a read overlaps it. R must be large enough that R + W > N.
R = 4 would make the sum 8, but it is the sum that matters and not R alone.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, a replicated store keeps answering every request from whichever replica each client can reach. What does it give up?
hints: A partition stops replicas from exchanging changes.
Ask what a client reads from a replica that has not received the latest change.

acceptedIdeas: Consistency, because some replies may be stale
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consistency, because some replies may be stale

questions.onCorrect: Replicas that cannot hear each other may hold different values, so a store that answers every request may return stale data, and that is the price of staying available.

misconceptions.feedback: A store that answers every request stays available. A store that refuses some requests to protect consistency is the other side of the choice.
Durability concerns whether a committed change survives a crash. A partition does not remove changes that have been stored; it only stops replicas from hearing about each other's.

choices.label: Durability, because committed writes are lost
Consistency, because some replies may be stale
Availability, because some requests are refused

questions.prompt: `authors` has the rows (1, 'Austen') and (2, 'Brontë'), written `(id, name)`. `books(id, title, writer, pages)` has the rows (11, 'Emma', 1, 474), (12, 'Persuasion', 1, 249) and (13, 'Jane Eyre', 2, 532). Which column of `books` is the foreign key?
hints: A foreign key holds a value that matches the key of a row in another table.
Compare the values in each column of `books` with the ids in `authors`.

acceptedIdeas: `writer`, because its values are ids of rows in `authors`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `writer`, because its values are ids of rows in `authors`

questions.onCorrect: The values 1 and 2 in `writer` are ids of rows in `authors`, so `writer` is the foreign key.

choices.label: `id`, because it identifies each book
`writer`, because its values are ids of rows in `authors`
`title`, because it is the column people read to find a book

misconceptions.feedback: The `id` column identifies the book itself. It is the table's own key and does not point at a row in another table.
A title names the book and is not an id from any other table. Look for the column whose values match the ids in `authors`.

questions.prompt: A gym lets members book classes. Its tables are `members`, `classes` and `bookings`, where each row of `bookings` is one member booked into one class. The gym also records whether each member attended each class they booked. Which table should hold the `attended` column?
hints: Ask whether attendance is a fact about the member, about the class, or about the pair.
Which table has one row for each member-class pair?

acceptedIdeas: `bookings`, because attendance describes the pair
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `bookings`, because attendance describes the pair

questions.onCorrect: Attendance describes one member in one class, which is the pair, so it is a column of the junction table.

choices.label: `bookings`, because attendance describes the pair
`classes`, because every class has an attendance record
`members`, because attendance is something a member does

misconceptions.feedback: A class has a different attendance for every member who booked it, so one `attended` column in the class's row cannot hold them all.
A member has a different attendance for every class they booked, so one `attended` column in the member's row cannot hold them all.

questions.prompt: A plan estimates 40 rows for a step, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reports 120,000 actual rows, which is 3,000 times as many. What does a gap of this size most likely say about the plan?
hints: Which numbers did the planner choose its strategy from?
The estimate comes from the statistics the planner holds.

choices.label: The step is slow only because it returned many rows, so the plan is sound
The estimates and the actual counts are meant to match exactly
The index on that table is corrupt
The statistics are stale or too coarse, and the joins above were chosen for 40 rows

acceptedIdeas: The statistics are stale or too coarse, and the joins above were chosen for 40 rows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The statistics are stale or too coarse, and the joins above were chosen for 40 rows

questions.onCorrect: The planner picked a join for 40 rows and got 120,000. The usual fix is to refresh the statistics and read the plan again.

misconceptions.feedback: The planner chose its strategy for 40 rows. Everything above this step was sized for a thousandth of the real data.
Estimates come from statistics and are approximate. A small gap is normal, and a gap of 3,000 times is a warning.
A wrong estimate is a statistics problem. A corrupt index would give wrong rows or an error.

questions.prompt: A transfer of 150 from A = 600 to B = 300 committed, and its commit record is in the log, but the table pages were never written. After recovery A = 450 and B = 450. Why does recovery produce these balances?
hints: Ask what survives the crash: the table pages or the log.
Recovery reads the log and looks for the commit record.

acceptedIdeas: Recovery replays the committed changes from the log, so both balances are updated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Recovery replays the committed changes from the log, so both balances are updated

questions.onCorrect: The commit record is in the log, so recovery replays both changes of the transfer and the balances come out at 450 and 450.

choices.label: Recovery replays the committed changes from the log, so both balances are updated
Commit forces every changed table page to disk, so the pages were already up to date
Recovery replays every record in the log, whether or not its transaction committed

misconceptions.feedback: Here the table pages were never written. A commit makes the log record durable, and not the table pages.
Recovery replays only the transactions whose commit record is present. A change without a commit record is discarded.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a transaction at Repeatable Read runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staff WHERE dept = 'A'` and gets 3. Another transaction then commits a new row with dept 'A'. What does the first transaction get if it runs the same count again?
hints: Ask when the snapshot of a Repeatable Read transaction is taken.
Ask which level takes one snapshot for the whole transaction, and which takes a fresh one for each statement.

acceptedIdeas: 3, because the transaction keeps the snapshot it began with
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 3, because the transaction keeps the snapshot it began with

questions.onCorrect: The second count reads the snapshot taken when the transaction began, so the committed row stays invisible and the result is still 3.

choices.label: 4, because the new row has been committed
An error, because the data changed under the transaction
3, because the transaction keeps the snapshot it began with

misconceptions.feedback: That is what Read Committed would give, where each statement takes a fresh snapshot. At Repeatable Read the whole transaction reads one snapshot.
Reading changed data causes no error. Repeatable Read aborts a transaction only when it tries to update a row that changed since its snapshot.

questions.prompt: A shop's product page shows the product with its customer reviews, and a popular product can collect hundreds of thousands of reviews. In a document store, how should the reviews be kept?
hints: Ask whether the reviews have a known upper size.
Every update to an embedded list rewrites the document that holds it.

acceptedIdeas: Referenced, with each review stored as its own document that links to the product
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Referenced, with each review stored as its own document that links to the product

questions.onCorrect: A collection without an upper bound is referenced, so each review is a separate document and the product document stays small.

choices.label: Referenced, with each review stored as its own document that links to the product
Embedded in the product document, so that one read returns the product with all its reviews
Embedded in the product document, because documents can grow as large as needed

misconceptions.feedback: A read that returned hundreds of thousands of reviews with the product would be slow, and every new review would rewrite the whole document. Data that grows without limit is referenced.
Documents have a size limit, such as 16 mebibytes in MongoDB, and every update to a growing document rewrites more data.

questions.prompt: A vet clinic describes itself like this: owners bring pets, each pet has a name and a species, and at every visit a vet weighs the pet and records the weight. There is one row for each visit. Where does the weight belong?
hints: Ask how many different weights one pet has over a year.
A column goes on the entity whose single row holds exactly one value for it.

choices.label: On the pet, because it is a fact about the pet
On the visit, because each visit has its own weight
On the vet, because the vet takes the measurement
As a new entity called Weight, because it is a noun in the description

acceptedIdeas: On the visit, because each visit has its own weight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On the visit, because each visit has its own weight

questions.onCorrect: The weight changes from visit to visit, so it describes the visit. Putting it on the pet would allow only one weight for the pet's whole life.

misconceptions.feedback: A pet weighs something different at each visit, so a single column on the pet would keep only the latest weight and overwrite the earlier ones. The fact belongs to one visit.
The vet only carries out the weighing. The number describes the animal on one day, and a vet would need a weight column for every pet seen.
A weight is a single value with nothing else recorded about it, so it is an attribute. A noun becomes an entity only when it is told apart one by one and has facts of its own.

questions.prompt: A bookshop describes how it works: customers place orders, each order lists books, and a book can appear on many orders. You are turning the description into tables. In what order do you work?
hints: You cannot decide how entities connect until you know what the entities are.
Cardinality needs both directions asked, and reading aloud checks the result.

items: Underline every noun in the description
Keep the nouns that are told apart one by one and have facts of their own as entities
Turn the remaining nouns into attributes of the entity each one describes
For each connection, ask how many of one side the other can have, in both directions
Read each connection aloud as a sentence to the shop owner

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nouns come first, then the test that sorts entities from attributes, then the cardinality of each connection asked both ways, and last a spoken check with the owner.

questions.onCorrect: Each step uses the result of the one before it, so entities have to be settled before cardinality, and the spoken reading is the last check.

questions.prompt: A bike-share records trips. Each trip is made by one rider on one bike. Over time a rider uses many bikes, and a bike is used by many riders. How are Rider and Bike connected?
hints: Ask the question in both directions: how many bikes can one rider use, and how many riders can one bike carry?
When both answers are many, the connection is stored in a table of its own.

choices.label: Many-to-many, with Trip as the entity between them
One-to-many, because every trip has one rider and one bike
One-to-one, because each trip pairs one rider with one bike

acceptedIdeas: Many-to-many, with Trip as the entity between them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many-to-many, with Trip as the entity between them

questions.onCorrect: Both directions are many, so the pair needs a table in between, and Trip is that table because it also records a time.

misconceptions.feedback: Each trip has one rider and one bike, but that describes Trip. Rider to Bike is asked across all trips, and a rider has many bikes while a bike has many riders.
A single trip pairs one rider with one bike, but a rider takes many trips on different bikes, so the pairing is not one-to-one over time.

questions.prompt: A gym's `bookings(member_id, class_id, booked_on)` has the primary key `(member_id, class_id)`. A member books the same class again the next week, and `INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, 5, '2026-11-09')` fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed: bookings.member_id, bookings.class_id`. Which change lets a member book the same class on different dates?
hints: The key lists the columns whose combination must be unique.
A second booking of the same class differs only in its date.

choices.label: Drop the primary key so that repeated pairs are accepted
Add an `id` column and keep `(member_id, class_id)` as the key
Make `booked_on` the primary key on its own
Add `booked_on` to the key: `(member_id, class_id, booked_on)`

acceptedIdeas: Add `booked_on` to the key: `(member_id, class_id, booked_on)`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add `booked_on` to the key: `(member_id, class_id, booked_on)`

questions.onCorrect: The key now holds the combination that really identifies a booking, so the same member and class can repeat on a new date and a duplicate on the same date is still refused.

misconceptions.feedback: Without a key nothing stops the same booking being entered twice by mistake, and rows can no longer be told apart.
The pair is still the key, so the same insert fails. An extra column does not change which combination has to be unique.
Two different members booking on the same date would collide, so one date cannot identify a booking.

questions.prompt: `students(id, name)` holds Ana (1), Ben (2), Chloe (3), Dev (4) and Eli (5). `enrollments(student_id, course_id)` holds (1,10), (1,11), (2,10), (3,10), (3,11), (3,12) and (5,12). The query `SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id` runs. How many rows does it return?
hints: The query groups the joined rows by student, so it returns one row for each student who appears in the join.
An inner join keeps a student only if some enrollments row matches their id.
Compare the student ids 1 to 5 with the ids that occur in the enrollments rows: 1, 2, 3 and 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ana, Ben, Chloe and Eli each have at least one enrollments row, so each forms a group. Dev has none, and the inner join drops a student with no match, so 4 rows come back: Ana 2, Ben 1, Chloe 3 and Eli 1.

questions.onCorrect: Dev has no enrollments row, so the inner join leaves Dev out of the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every student. The inner join keeps a student only when some enrollments row has their id, and Dev has none.
That counts the enrollments rows. The query groups them by student, so it returns one row per student.

questions.prompt: A shop sells products. An order can include many products, a product appears on many orders, and each order records a quantity of each product it includes. Which design stores this?
hints: The quantity describes one product on one order, not an order or a product alone.
Many-to-many relationships are stored as a table with a row for each pair.

choices.label: `orders(id, product_ids)` and `products(id)`, with a list of ids in each order
`products(id, order_id, quantity)`, with the order on each product
`orders(id)`, `products(id)` and `order_lines(order_id, product_id, quantity)`
`orders(id, quantity)` and `products(id, quantity)`

acceptedIdeas: `orders(id)`, `products(id)` and `order_lines(order_id, product_id, quantity)`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `orders(id)`, `products(id)` and `order_lines(order_id, product_id, quantity)`

questions.onCorrect: A row of `order_lines` is one product on one order, so the quantity has exactly one value there.

misconceptions.feedback: Several ids in one cell cannot be joined or checked by a foreign key, and a quantity for each product has nowhere to go.
A product row could then belong to one order only, so a product sold on two orders would need two product rows.
A quantity on either table cannot say how many of which product went on which order. The amount belongs to the pair.

questions.prompt: `products(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT, name TEXT)` uses a generated `id` as its key, and the shop's rule is that no two products share an `sku`. Running `INSERT INTO products(sku, name) VALUES ('P-100', 'Pen')` twice succeeds both times, and `SELECT sku, COUNT(*) FROM products GROUP BY sku` returns `('P-100', 2)`. What is missing?
hints: Which column is the business rule about?
A surrogate key identifies rows for the database and leaves the natural identifier unprotected.

choices.label: Nothing, because the generated `id` already makes each row unique
A foreign key from `sku` to a second table of products
A `UNIQUE` constraint on `sku`, and `NOT NULL` if needed
A `CHECK` constraint on `name` that rejects repeated names

acceptedIdeas: A `UNIQUE` constraint on `sku`, and `NOT NULL` if needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A `UNIQUE` constraint on `sku`, and `NOT NULL` if needed

questions.onCorrect: A surrogate key keeps references stable, and the natural identifier still needs its own `UNIQUE` constraint, or duplicates arrive unchecked.

misconceptions.feedback: The generated id is unique whatever the other columns hold. It says nothing about `sku`, so two rows can share one.
A foreign key checks that a value exists elsewhere. It does not stop the same value occurring twice in this table.
The rule concerns `sku`, and a check on one row's `name` cannot see the other rows.

questions.prompt: `orders(id, customer_id, total)` has a foreign key `customer_id` to `customers(id)` declared `ON DELETE CASCADE`. `customers` holds Ana (1) and Ben (2). `orders` holds (101, 1, 20), (102, 1, 35), (103, 2, 10) and (104, 2, 5). `DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1` runs. How many rows does `orders` hold afterwards?
hints: Find which `orders` rows have `customer_id = 1`.
`ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes every row that refers to the deleted row.
Four orders minus the ones that refer to customer 1 leaves the ones for customer 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cascade deletes the orders that refer to the deleted customer. Orders 101 and 102 belong to Ana, so 103 and 104 remain: 2 rows.

questions.onCorrect: A cascade is convenient and removes rows without asking, so it suits data that has no meaning without its parent.

misconceptions.feedback: That would mean the delete changed nothing in `orders`. With `ON DELETE CASCADE`, the orders of the deleted customer are deleted with it.
A cascade removes every order of the customer, not one. Ana has two orders, and both go.

questions.prompt: `orders.customer_id` references `customers(id)`. The business must keep every order for seven years, so deleting a customer who still has orders has to fail and leave the orders alone. Which foreign key action fits?
hints: Decide whether the delete should succeed, and what should happen to the child rows if it does.
One action refuses the delete, one removes the children and one detaches them.

choices.label: `ON DELETE CASCADE`, which deletes the customer's orders with the customer
`ON DELETE RESTRICT`, which refuses the delete while orders exist
`ON DELETE SET NULL`, which keeps the orders and clears their `customer_id`
No foreign key at all, so the delete is never refused

acceptedIdeas: `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, which refuses the delete while orders exist
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, which refuses the delete while orders exist

questions.onCorrect: In SQLite, deleting a customer who still has orders under this rule fails with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`, and the orders remain.

misconceptions.feedback: The cascade would erase the orders the business must keep, and without any warning.
The orders stay, but they no longer say whose they are, and the delete succeeds when it is meant to fail.
Nothing then stops a customer vanishing while orders still point at the missing id.

questions.prompt: `enrol_flat(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, grade)` has one row for each student on each course. Each of these is a problem with the table. Which kind of anomaly is each?
hints: Ask whether the problem is changing a fact, adding a fact or removing a fact.
A delete anomaly loses a fact you did not mean to delete, and an insert anomaly cannot store a fact without another one.

items.label: Ben changes his name, which appears on four rows, and one of the four is missed
items.explanation: One fact is stored in four places, so a change can reach some of them and not the others.

items.label: A course is renamed and only some of its rows are changed
items.explanation: The title is repeated on every enrolment row, so the old and new titles now exist together.

items.label: A new course, Graphics, cannot be stored until a student enrols on it
items.explanation: A row needs a student, so a fact about a course alone has nowhere to go.

items.label: Dev is admitted but has chosen no course, so there is no row to hold his name
items.explanation: A row needs a course, so a fact about a student alone has nowhere to go.

items.label: Chloe is the only student on Compilers, and deleting her row also deletes the title Compilers
items.explanation: The title was stored only in her row, so removing the row removes the fact.

items.label: Course 11 is cancelled and its rows are deleted, which removes the only record of two students' names
items.explanation: The names were stored only on rows for that course, so deleting those rows deletes them.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben's name and the renamed course are update anomalies, Graphics and Dev are insert anomalies, and Compilers and the two students' names are delete anomalies.

questions.onCorrect: All three come from facts about different things sharing one row, so one fact cannot be stored, changed or removed on its own.

questions.prompt: `staff_flat(staff_id, name, dept, dept_head)` holds (1, Ana, Sales, Kim), (2, Ben, Sales, Kim), (3, Cy, Ops, Lee), (4, Dee, Ops, Pat) and (5, Eve, Sales, Kim). The designer expects each of these dependencies to hold. Which one do the rows break?
hints: A dependency `A` → `B` breaks when one value of `A` appears with two different values of `B`.
Look for a department that appears with more than one head.

choices.label: `staff_id` → `dept`, because staff 1 and 2 share Sales
`dept` → `dept_head`, because Ops appears with Lee and Pat
`dept_head` → `dept`, because Kim leads Sales on three rows
`staff_id` → `name`, because two staff could share a name

acceptedIdeas: `dept` → `dept_head`, because Ops appears with Lee and Pat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `dept` → `dept_head`, because Ops appears with Lee and Pat

questions.onCorrect: Ops appears with two heads, so `dept` does not determine `dept_head` in these rows. Rows can disprove a dependency, but they can never prove one.

misconceptions.feedback: Each staff_id appears once, so it does fix a department. Two staff sharing a department does not break this arrow.
Kim appears only with Sales, Lee only with Ops and Pat only with Ops, so each head fixes one department.
Every staff_id appears once with one name. Names repeating would not break this arrow.

questions.prompt: A team keeps `orders_flat` as it is and adds application code that updates every row for a customer whenever an email changes. Later, a maintenance script updates the email on a single order. What does the table do?
hints: Is the rule that rows agree written in the table or only in the code?
A script that skips the application code skips the rule.

choices.label: It refuses the change, because the rows of one customer must agree
It updates the customer's other rows too, as the application code does
It accepts the change and now holds two emails for one customer
It repairs the difference at the next commit

acceptedIdeas: It accepts the change and now holds two emails for one customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It accepts the change and now holds two emails for one customer

questions.onCorrect: A rule kept only in one program holds only for that program. Putting each fact in one place needs no rule, because a single copy cannot disagree with itself.

misconceptions.feedback: The table has no rule saying that a customer's rows must agree, so it cannot refuse the update.
The application code runs only when it is called. The database copies nothing on its own.
A commit saves changes and never reconciles them, so the two addresses stay.

questions.prompt: Each description gives a table, its key and its dependencies. Each normal form includes the ones before it. Which form does each table fail first, or is it already in third normal form?
hints: Test the forms in order: first a single value in each cell, then dependence on the whole key, then dependence on nothing but the key.
A column that depends on part of a composite key fails 2NF, and a column that depends on a non-key column fails 3NF.

items.label: `contacts(person_id, phones)`, where one cell of `phones` holds '555-0101, 555-0102'
items.explanation: A cell holds a list, so the column is not atomic.

items.label: `order_lines(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name)`, key `(order_id, product_id)`, where `product_id` → `product_name`
items.explanation: `product_name` depends on part of the key.

items.label: `enrolments(student_id, course_id, grade, student_name)`, key `(student_id, course_id)`, where `student_id` → `student_name`
items.explanation: `student_name` depends on `student_id`, which is only part of the key.

items.label: `employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name)`, key `emp_id`, where `dept_id` → `dept_name`
items.explanation: The key is one column, so no partial dependency exists, but a non-key column depends on another non-key column.

items.label: `orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_city)`, key `order_id`, where `customer_id` → `customer_city`
items.explanation: `customer_city` depends on `customer_id`, which is not a key of this table.

items.label: `order_lines(order_id, product_id, qty)`, key `(order_id, product_id)`, with no other dependency
items.explanation: `qty` depends on the whole key and on nothing else.

items.label: `products(product_id, name, price)`, key `product_id`
items.explanation: Every column depends on the key alone.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contacts table fails 1NF; the order lines with a name and the enrolments with a student name fail 2NF; the employees and orders tables fail 3NF; the plain order lines and products are in 3NF.

questions.onCorrect: Each form removes a pattern the previous one allows, so the first one a table fails tells you which split to make.

questions.prompt: The table `t(employee, project, skill)` holds (Ana, P1, SQL), (Ana, P2, Rust) and (Ben, P1, Rust). It is cut into `ep(employee, project)` and `ps(project, skill)`, and the pieces are joined on `project`. The join returns (Ana, P1, Rust), (Ana, P1, SQL), (Ana, P2, Rust), (Ben, P1, Rust) and (Ben, P1, SQL). How many of those rows were not in `t`?
hints: Compare each returned row with the three rows of `t`.
A row in the join but not in `t` is a spurious row.
Project P1 appears with two skills and with two employees, so the join pairs every employee on P1 with every skill on P1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three of the five returned rows are in the original: (Ana, P1, SQL), (Ana, P2, Rust) and (Ben, P1, Rust). The other two, (Ana, P1, Rust) and (Ben, P1, SQL), were never there, so 2 rows are invented.

questions.onCorrect: Project P1 has two employees and two skills, so the join pairs all four, and two of the four pairings were never recorded.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the whole join. Some of those rows were in the original table.
That is the number of rows in the original. The question asks how many returned rows are new.

questions.prompt: `staff_flat(staff_id, name, dept, dept_head)` holds (1, Ana, Sales, Kim), (2, Ben, Sales, Kim), (3, Cy, Ops, Lee) and (4, Dee, Support, Kim), with `dept` → `dept_head`. It is cut into two tables that are joined on their shared column. Which cut gives back exactly the four rows and stores each department's head only once?
hints: A cut is lossless when the shared column is a key of one of the pieces.
The goal is also that `dept_head` is stored once for each department.

choices.label: `(staff_id, name)` and `(dept, dept_head)`
`(staff_id, name, dept_head)` and `(dept, dept_head)`
`(staff_id, name, dept)` and `(dept, dept_head)`
`(staff_id, name, dept, dept_head)` and `(dept, dept_head)`

acceptedIdeas: `(staff_id, name, dept)` and `(dept, dept_head)`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `(staff_id, name, dept)` and `(dept, dept_head)`

questions.onCorrect: `dept` is the key of the second table, so each staff row finds exactly one department row, and the head sits only there.

misconceptions.feedback: The pieces share no column, so there is nothing to join on. Pairing them anyway gives 12 rows, and the link between a person and a department is lost.
The shared column `dept_head` is a key of neither piece, and Kim leads two departments. Joining returns 7 rows, so 3 are invented.
The join returns the four rows, but the head is still repeated in the staff piece, so the anomaly remains.

questions.prompt: A weekly sales report joins `fact_sales`, with 80 million rows, to `dim_product` and `dim_date`, and takes 40 seconds. A teammate proposes copying `category` and `month` into every fact row so the report needs no joins. What should the team do first?
hints: Which step of the query actually takes the 40 seconds?
Denormalising is a decision made after measuring.

choices.label: Copy the columns now, because every join is slow on a large table
Merge the three tables into one, because a star schema suits only small data
Measure the query with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before changing the schema
Move the report to a key-value store, because it has no joins

acceptedIdeas: Measure the query with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before changing the schema
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Measure the query with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before changing the schema

questions.onCorrect: The plan shows where the time goes. If it is a missing index or stale statistics, the copy would have cost a lot and changed nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: A join on indexed keys is often cheap, and the 40 seconds may come from somewhere else. The copy would also add 80 million places to update when a category is renamed.
A star schema is built for large fact tables. Merging copies every description into every fact row.
A key-value store cannot group and sum by category without reading every value, so the report would get slower.

questions.prompt: A shop's database serves two kinds of work. Which kind is each of these?
hints: Ask how many rows the work reads and whether it writes.
Reporting groups many rows by dimensions such as category, region and month.

bins.label: Transactions: many small reads and writes
Reporting: few large reads over many rows

items.label: Saving a customer's order and its lines
items.explanation: It writes a few rows and must be fast and safe.

items.label: Looking up one order by its number to show its status
items.explanation: It reads one row by key.

items.label: Reducing a product's stock by one when it sells
items.explanation: It changes one row and is repeated thousands of times a day.

items.label: Summing revenue for every category over the last twelve months
items.explanation: It reads millions of fact rows and groups them.

items.label: Counting orders for each region and week for a dashboard
items.explanation: It scans a long period and groups by two dimensions.

items.label: Finding the ten best-selling products of the year across all stores
items.explanation: It aggregates the whole fact table before ranking.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Saving an order, looking up an order and reducing stock are transactions, and the revenue sum, the regional count and the best-seller ranking are reporting.

questions.onCorrect: The two kinds pull the design in opposite directions: transactions favour one copy of each fact, and reports favour a fact table with dimensions around it.

questions.prompt: `orders.total` is a copy of the sum of an order's item amounts, kept so that the order list does not need to add them up. Items change from several places in the application. Which way of keeping the copy correct is the most reliable?
hints: A copy stays right only if the database itself updates it, or if something checks it.
Who is responsible for the copy when a new code path is added next year?

choices.label: Update both in one transaction or a trigger, and check for drift nightly
Rely on each developer remembering to update the total with every item change
Recompute the total only when a customer reports a wrong amount
Remove the foreign key between orders and items so that they cannot conflict

acceptedIdeas: Update both in one transaction or a trigger, and check for drift nightly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Update both in one transaction or a trigger, and check for drift nightly

questions.onCorrect: Updating in one transaction or a trigger covers every code path, and the nightly comparison catches any drift that still gets through.

misconceptions.feedback: One missed code path leaves a total that disagrees with its items, and nothing notices.
Wrong totals would reach customers first and stay wrong until someone complains.
The foreign key stops items pointing at a missing order. Removing it adds a different fault and does not keep the total right.

questions.prompt: An `orders` table has 60 million rows and 12 columns, and takes 2,000 inserts a second. A teammate adds a B-tree index on every column so that any filter will be fast. What is the likely result?
hints: What has to happen to an index when a row is added?
An index helps queries that match few rows on its column and costs something on every write.

choices.label: Every query gets faster, because the planner always uses the best index
Filters get faster, but each insert updates 12 indexes and storage grows
Inserts are unaffected, because an index is built once when it is created
Inserts get faster, because the indexes keep the rows sorted in advance

acceptedIdeas: Filters get faster, but each insert updates 12 indexes and storage grows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Filters get faster, but each insert updates 12 indexes and storage grows

questions.onCorrect: Each index is a second copy of a column that must be maintained, so the right set is the few indexes the queries actually use.

misconceptions.feedback: A query that matches a large share of the table is still read faster by a scan, so the planner skips an index there.
An index is kept up to date, so each insert adds an entry to every one of them.
Sorted indexes make lookups cheaper and make each insert more expensive, because it has to find its place in each tree.

questions.prompt: A query asks for the order with `id = 41250000`, and `id` has a B-tree index. In what order are the pages read?
hints: The search starts at the top of the tree and narrows at every level.
The table itself is read last, once the index has said where the row is.

items: The root page of the index
An internal page of the index, chosen by comparing the key with the root's entries
The leaf page of the index that holds the entry for the key
The table page that the entry points to

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The root narrows to an internal page, the internal page narrows to a leaf, the leaf entry points to a table page, and the table page holds the row.

questions.onCorrect: Each level cuts the search to one child page, so the number of pages read grows with the height of the tree, plus one for the table.

questions.prompt: `SELECT * FROM events WHERE country = 'NL'` has no index. On a laptop with 2,000 rows it is instant. In production, with 150 million rows, the same query takes minutes. Why?
hints: Compare the number of pages a scan reads in each place.
With no index, the only way to find the rows is to read them all.
