choices.label: The production server must have slower hardware than the laptop
The planner used an index in development and ignores it in production
Larger tables are slower because the planner stops optimising them
A scan reads every page, so the work grows with the table

acceptedIdeas: A scan reads every page, so the work grows with the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A scan reads every page, so the work grows with the table

questions.onCorrect: A scan costs one read per page, so it was cheap on 2,000 rows and expensive on 150 million. An index on `country` would keep the cost near the number of matching rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Hardware differs by a small factor. The table is about 75,000 times bigger, and a scan reads all of it.
There is no index on `country` in either place, so both read the whole table.
The planner works the same way. A scan simply has more pages to read.

questions.prompt: `users(id, email, name)` has 2,000 rows and an index `idx_email` on `email`. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` prints `SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_email (email=?)` for `WHERE email = 'u5@Example.org'`, and `SCAN users` for `WHERE lower(email) = 'u5@example.org'`. How do you make the second query use an index?
hints: The index holds `email` values in sorted order, and the condition asks about a different value.
An index can be built on an expression.

choices.label: Create an index on the expression `lower(email)`
Add a second index on `email` under another name
Run `ANALYZE` so that the planner notices `idx_email`
Select fewer columns instead of `*`

acceptedIdeas: Create an index on the expression `lower(email)`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Create an index on the expression `lower(email)`

questions.onCorrect: After the expression index, the plan reads `SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_email_lower (<expr>=?)`. A function applied to an indexed column hides the column from its own index.

misconceptions.feedback: A second index on the same column is sorted the same way. It still cannot answer a condition on `lower(email)`.
Statistics help the planner choose between usable indexes. This index is not usable, because it is sorted by `email` and the condition asks about `lower(email)`.
The columns selected do not decide whether the condition can use the index.

questions.prompt: `emp(id, last_name, first_name, salary, dept)` has one index, `idx_name` on `(last_name, first_name)`. For each filter, does SQLite seek on the index, or read the whole table? Each result comes from `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`.
hints: An index can seek only when the condition fixes or bounds its leading column in the stored form.
A function on the column, a leading wildcard and a condition on the second column alone each remove the starting point.

items.label: `last_name = 'L3'`
items.explanation: `SEARCH emp USING INDEX idx_name (last_name=?)`: the leading column is fixed.

items.label: `last_name = 'L3' AND first_name = 'F3'`
items.explanation: `SEARCH emp USING INDEX idx_name (last_name=? AND first_name=?)`: both columns narrow the search.

items.label: `last_name = 'L3' AND first_name >= 'F2'`
items.explanation: `SEARCH emp USING INDEX idx_name (last_name=? AND first_name>?)`: equality on the first column, then a range.

items.label: `last_name >= 'L2' AND last_name < 'L3'`
items.explanation: `SEARCH emp USING INDEX idx_name (last_name>? AND last_name<?)`: a range on the leading column.

items.label: `first_name = 'F3'`
items.explanation: `SCAN emp`: the second column alone has no starting point in the index.

items.label: `last_name LIKE '%3'`
items.explanation: `SCAN emp`: a pattern that begins with a wildcard cannot use the sort order.

items.label: `upper(last_name) = 'L3'`
items.explanation: `SCAN emp`: the function hides the column.

items.label: `last_name = 'L3' OR first_name = 'F3'`
items.explanation: `SCAN emp`: the second branch cannot seek, so the whole table is read.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The four filters on the leading column, with or without a second condition, seek; the filter on first_name alone, the leading wildcard, upper() and the OR read the whole table.

questions.onCorrect: The seek needs a starting point in the sort order of the leading column, and the plan line shows the columns it used.

questions.prompt: `SELECT last_name, first_name, salary FROM emp WHERE last_name = 'L3'` has the plan `SEARCH emp USING INDEX idx_name (last_name=?)`, so each match still needs a visit to the table for `salary`. Which change lets the query be answered from the index alone?
hints: A covering index holds every column the query reads.
Which column is the plan visiting the table for?

choices.label: Change the query to `SELECT *`, so the index serves every column
Add a second index on `salary` alone
Index `(last_name, first_name, salary)` to cover the query
Run `ANALYZE emp` to refresh the statistics

acceptedIdeas: Index `(last_name, first_name, salary)` to cover the query
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Index `(last_name, first_name, salary)` to cover the query

questions.onCorrect: With `salary` in the index, the plan becomes `SEARCH emp USING COVERING INDEX idx_name_sal (last_name=?)`, and the table is not read.

misconceptions.feedback: More columns make it less likely that an index holds everything the query reads.
The query filters on `last_name`, so an index on `salary` is not used, and the table visit remains.
Statistics change estimates. They do not add `salary` to any index.

questions.prompt:
This plan comes from the PostgreSQL documentation for a join of `tenk1 t1` and `tenk2 t2`.
`Nested Loop  (cost=4.65..118.50 rows=10 width=488) (actual time=0.017..0.051 rows=10.00 loops=1)`
`  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on tenk1 t1  (cost=4.36..39.38 rows=10 width=244) (actual time=0.009..0.017 rows=10.00 loops=1)`
`  ->  Index Scan using tenk2_unique2 on tenk2 t2  (cost=0.29..7.90 rows=1 width=244) (actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1.00 loops=10)`
The inner `Index Scan` shows `rows=1.00 loops=10`. What does that mean?
hints: In a nested loop, the inner side runs once for each row of the outer side.
Actual rows are reported per loop, so multiply by loops for the total.

choices.label: The index was searched once and returned 1 row
The index was searched 10 times and returned 1 row each, 10 in all
The index was searched 10 times and returned 10 rows each, 100 rows in all
The index was searched once and returned 10 rows

acceptedIdeas: The index was searched 10 times and returned 1 row each, 10 in all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The index was searched 10 times and returned 1 row each, 10 in all

questions.onCorrect: The outer side gave 10 rows, so the inner index search ran 10 times at one row each, which is why a nested loop suits a small outer side with an indexed inner side.

misconceptions.feedback: `loops=10` says the step ran 10 times, once for each row of the outer side.
`rows` is the average for one run of the step, so one row each time and 10 in total.
The 10 is the number of runs. The row count shown is per run.

questions.prompt: `orders` has 3,000 rows, 30 of them with `status = 'open'`, and `customers` has 200 rows. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT c.name, o.total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'open'` prints `SCAN o` and `SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)`. Which change cuts the work most?
hints: Which step reads the most rows?
The filter that keeps 30 of 3,000 rows is the one an index could use.

choices.label: Index `orders(status)`, so the loop starts from the 30 open orders
Index `customers(name)`, because the query selects the name
Index `customers(id)`, because the join uses it
Write `customers` first in the query, so that it is the outer table

acceptedIdeas: Index `orders(status)`, so the loop starts from the 30 open orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Index `orders(status)`, so the loop starts from the 30 open orders

questions.onCorrect: With the index, the plan becomes `SEARCH o USING INDEX idx_o_status (status=?)`, so the loop runs 30 times and not 3,000, with one primary key lookup into `customers` each time.

misconceptions.feedback: The name is only read after the join has found the row. The join already finds each customer through the primary key.
`id` is the primary key, and the plan already says the lookup in `customers` uses it.
The planner chooses the join order itself, and the cost is in reading all 3,000 orders, whichever order is written.

questions.prompt: A report query is slow, and you suspect the planner is working from poor estimates. In what order do you work?
hints: You need the actual rows before you can compare them with the estimates.
Check the effect of the fix by running the same measurement again.

items: Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the slow query
Compare the estimated and actual rows at each step
Find the first step where the two differ by a large factor
Refresh the statistics on that table with `ANALYZE`
Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` again and check whether the plan changed

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, compare estimates with actuals, locate the first large gap, refresh the statistics for that table and measure again.

questions.onCorrect: The first large gap is where the plan went wrong, since everything above it was planned from that estimate.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a transaction runs `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A'` and the `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint fails, because A holds 50. The application ignores the error and sends `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'B'` in the same transaction. What happens?
hints: What state is a PostgreSQL transaction in after a statement fails?
Money is conserved only if the debit and the credit stand or fall together.

choices.label: B is credited and `COMMIT` saves it, because the failed debit changed nothing
B is credited, and the debit is retried automatically at `COMMIT`
The credit is refused, because the transaction is aborted until `ROLLBACK`
The credit runs, and only the debit is rolled back

acceptedIdeas: The credit is refused, because the transaction is aborted until `ROLLBACK`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The credit is refused, because the transaction is aborted until `ROLLBACK`

questions.onCorrect: The failed debit aborts the transaction, so the credit cannot run and nothing is kept. Debit and credit stand or fall together, which is atomicity.

misconceptions.feedback: That would create 100 from nothing. After the error the transaction takes no further commands.
The database never retries a failed statement for you. The transaction is already aborted.
PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction on an error. It does not keep the half that succeeded.

questions.prompt: A transaction moves 150 from A to B and commits. In what order do these things happen?
hints: The log is written before the table pages, and the client is told only when the commit record is safe.
Table pages are written after COMMIT has already returned.

items: The changes are described in log records
The commit record is written to the log
The log is flushed to disk
`COMMIT` returns to the client
The changed table pages are written out later, at a checkpoint

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The changes go into log records, the commit record follows, the log is flushed, COMMIT then returns, and the table pages are written afterwards.

questions.onCorrect: Only the log has to reach the disk before COMMIT returns, because recovery can rebuild the table pages from it.

questions.prompt: A transfer debits A and credits B as two statements in one transaction. The credit fails, but the debit stays committed and 100 has vanished. Which ACID property failed?
hints: Which property says that all of a transaction's changes happen or none do?
Durability, isolation and consistency each answer a different failure.

choices.label: Durability, because a committed debit was lost
Atomicity, because the debit was kept without the credit
Isolation, because the two statements ran at the same time
Consistency, because the total changed and no rule can allow that

acceptedIdeas: Atomicity, because the debit was kept without the credit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atomicity, because the debit was kept without the credit

questions.onCorrect: Atomicity makes the two statements one unit, so either both are kept or neither is.

misconceptions.feedback: The debit was not lost. It was kept, and durability concerns whether committed work survives a crash.
The statements ran one after the other in one transaction. Isolation concerns separate transactions overlapping.
The total changing is the symptom. The cause is that the transaction was split, which is what atomicity guards against.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which of these can happen at which levels? Sort each anomaly by what the PostgreSQL documentation says about Read Committed and Repeatable Read.
hints: Repeatable Read gives the whole transaction one snapshot.
Write skew needs a level that checks what each transaction read.

bins.label: Read Committed allows it, Repeatable Read does not
Read Committed and Repeatable Read both allow it

items.label: A non-repeatable read
items.explanation: Read Committed lets a later statement see rows committed since the transaction began, and Repeatable Read keeps one snapshot.

items.label: A phantom read
items.explanation: Repeatable Read keeps one snapshot, so in PostgreSQL a repeated count of a range does not change.

items.label: A lost update from reading a value and writing it back
items.explanation: At Repeatable Read the second writer is refused with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'.

items.label: Write skew between two transactions that update different rows
items.explanation: Neither level notices, because the transactions write different rows. Only Serializable prevents it.

items.label: A dirty read of another transaction's uncommitted change
items.explanation: PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data, even though the standard allows it at the lowest level.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Non-repeatable reads, phantoms and read-then-write lost updates happen at Read Committed only; write skew happens at both levels; dirty reads happen at no PostgreSQL level.

questions.onCorrect: Each higher level removes a group of anomalies, and write skew survives until Serializable.

questions.prompt: `oncall(doctor, on_call)` holds Ana and Ben, both on call, and a rule says at least one doctor must stay on call. At Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL, Ana's session and Ben's session each run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall WHERE on_call` and get 2. Each then sets only its own row to false and commits, and both commits succeed. Nobody is on call. Which anomaly is this, and what stops it?
hints: Did the two transactions write the same row?
Each transaction followed the rule on what it read, and the rule broke across them.

choices.label: A lost update, which Repeatable Read prevents by aborting one transaction
A phantom read, which Repeatable Read prevents in PostgreSQL
A dirty read, which Read Committed prevents
Write skew, which only Serializable prevents

acceptedIdeas: Write skew, which only Serializable prevents
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write skew, which only Serializable prevents

questions.onCorrect: Each transaction was right about its own snapshot, and together they broke the rule. In PostgreSQL, Serializable aborts one of them with a serialization failure.

misconceptions.feedback: The two transactions wrote different rows, so neither overwrote the other, and Repeatable Read has no conflict to detect.
No new rows appeared. Each transaction changed an existing row after reading a count.
Neither transaction saw uncommitted data. Each read committed data that was true when read.

questions.prompt: A report runs `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments` at the start of one transaction and again at the end, and the two totals have to agree while other transactions keep committing new payments. In PostgreSQL, what is the lowest isolation level that guarantees this?
hints: Which levels give the whole transaction one snapshot?
In PostgreSQL, Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads.

choices.label: Repeatable Read, because both queries use the same snapshot
Read Committed, because each query sees only committed data
Serializable, because lower levels allow phantom reads in PostgreSQL
Read Uncommitted, because it never waits for other transactions

acceptedIdeas: Repeatable Read, because both queries use the same snapshot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Repeatable Read, because both queries use the same snapshot

questions.onCorrect: A snapshot taken at the first statement is used for the whole transaction, so new payments committed in between are invisible to it.

misconceptions.feedback: Committed data can change between the two queries. Each statement takes a fresh view of what has been committed.
PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read does not allow phantoms, so the lower level already gives the same total twice.
In PostgreSQL it behaves like Read Committed, so it does not keep the total steady.

questions.prompt: At Read Committed, a payment service runs `SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 7`, adds 30 in application code and runs `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 130 WHERE id = 7`. Two requests do this at the same time, and the account gains only 30 and not 60. What is the most direct fix?
hints: The loss happens between the read and the write, when each request holds an old value.
An update that computes the new value itself uses the row's current value after waiting for the lock.

choices.label: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE id = 7`, so the database adds
Wrap the two statements in `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, since Read Committed stops lost updates in a transaction
Add an index on `accounts.balance` so that the update runs faster
Read the balance twice and compare the two values before writing

acceptedIdeas: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE id = 7`, so the database adds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE id = 7`, so the database adds

questions.onCorrect: The second update waits for the row lock and then adds 30 to the new balance, so both additions count.

misconceptions.feedback: Both requests can still read the same balance before either writes, and Read Committed does not detect that.
A faster update leaves the stale read in place, and speed only narrows the window.
The balance can still change between the second read and the write.

questions.prompt: An application saves an account with a version column. In what order does one save go, when another user has changed the row in between?
hints: The version is noted when the row is read and checked when it is written.
The count of rows updated is how the application learns of a conflict.

items: Read the row and note its version, 3
Work out the new balance in the application
Run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 130, version = 4 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3`
Check how many rows the update reported
If it reported 0 rows, read the row again and start over

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Read the row and its version, compute the new value, run the update with the old version in its WHERE clause, check the row count and re-read and retry when it is 0.

questions.onCorrect: The `WHERE version = 3` clause matches nothing once someone else has saved, so a count of 0 rows means another user got there first.

questions.prompt: A user opens an edit form for an order, goes for a coffee and saves ten minutes later. Another user may edit the same order during that time. How should the application guard against overwriting?
hints: How long would a lock have to be held?
What does the application need to learn at the moment of saving?

choices.label: Run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` when the form opens and hold the lock until the save
Do nothing, because Read Committed stops a save overwriting someone else's change
Keep a version column and check it when saving
Run the whole session at Serializable so the second save waits

acceptedIdeas: Keep a version column and check it when saving
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep a version column and check it when saving

questions.onCorrect: No lock is held while the user thinks. At the save, a changed version tells the application someone else edited the row, and it can ask the user to review.

misconceptions.feedback: The row would stay locked for the whole coffee break, and everyone else who wants it would wait.
Read Committed lets the later save replace the earlier one, as both write values built from an old read.
A transaction cannot sensibly stay open across a person's break, and the second save would be aborted, not made to wait.

questions.prompt: A shop stores each order as one document with its lines embedded, and each line copies the product name and unit price at the time of the sale. Later a product is renamed and repriced. What should happen to the old orders?
hints: What does an order need to remember about the product?
Does the old price belong to the product or to the sale?

choices.label: Every old order should be updated, because copies must always match
The lines should hold only the product id, so old orders show the new name and price
The orders should move to a relational database, where nothing is copied
Nothing, because an order records what was sold at the time

acceptedIdeas: Nothing, because an order records what was sold at the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing, because an order records what was sold at the time

questions.onCorrect: Some copies are the data. The price on an order line is a fact about the sale and not about the product, so it must not follow later changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Rewriting history changes what the customer was charged. The copy is deliberate here.
Old orders would then show a price that was never charged, and their totals would change.
A relational design would still need to store the price paid with each line, because a product's price changes.

questions.prompt: Which kind of store fits each of these workloads best?
hints: Ask how the data is read: by one key, as one unit, or across many relationships.
Rules and transactions across rows point to a relational database.

items.label: Login sessions fetched by session id on every request and expiring after 30 minutes
items.explanation: Every read is a lookup by one key, and nothing is searched by content.

items.label: A counter of page visits that is incremented thousands of times a second
items.explanation: One key, one atomic increment.

items.label: Product pages that show a product with its photos and specifications as one unit
items.explanation: The data is read together, so one document means one read.

items.label: Blog posts with at most a few dozen comments that are always shown with the post
items.explanation: The comments are few and bounded, so they embed in the post.

items.label: Bank transfers between accounts that need rules and atomic updates across rows
items.explanation: Constraints and transactions across rows are what the relational model offers.

items.label: A school timetable in which rooms, teachers and classes are joined in many different ways
items.explanation: Queries cross many relationships that cannot be known in advance.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sessions and visit counters suit a key-value store, product pages and blog posts a document store, and bank transfers and the timetable a relational database.

questions.onCorrect: The access pattern decides. Single-key reads, whole-unit reads and queries across relationships each have a natural home.

questions.prompt: A key-value store keeps sessions under keys such as `session:9f3a`, each value holding a user id and an expiry. Support wants every session of user 7. The store looks values up by key and has no other index. What do you do?
hints: What can the store find quickly?
If the question is asked often, build the answer in advance.

choices.label: Read every session value and filter on the user id, which is cheap because lookups are fast
Keep a second key that lists user 7's session keys, and update it as sessions start and end
Rely on the store to index the user id inside each value, as a relational database would

acceptedIdeas: Keep a second key that lists user 7's session keys, and update it as sessions start and end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep a second key that lists user 7's session keys, and update it as sessions start and end

questions.onCorrect: The application keeps its own index as another key. It costs an extra write on every change, and it makes the lookup by user a single read.

misconceptions.feedback: Each lookup is fast, but one is needed for every session in the store, which amounts to a full scan.
A key-value store treats the value as opaque and builds no index on its contents.

questions.prompt: A store has N = 5 replicas, writes are acknowledged by W = 2 and reads ask R = 3. A client reads straight after a write. Is the read guaranteed to include the latest value?
hints: Compute R + W and compare it with N.
Can you pick 3 replicas out of 5 that avoid the 2 with the write?

choices.label: No, because R + W = 5 does not exceed N
Yes, because R + W equals N, so every replica is covered
No, because reads are consistent only if every replica is asked
No, because reads are only consistent when every replica is asked

acceptedIdeas: No, because R + W = 5 does not exceed N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because R + W = 5 does not exceed N

questions.onCorrect: Three replicas can be chosen from the three that missed the write, so the read may return an old value.

misconceptions.feedback: A majority read overlaps a majority write. Here W = 2 is not a majority, so the replicas asked can all lack the write.
The sum has to exceed N. Equal to N leaves a choice of three replicas that avoids both of the two with the write.
Asking every replica is enough but not needed. R + W > N already guarantees an overlap.

questions.prompt: An `events` table is split over 8 shards by range of `created_at`, so that each shard holds one month. Writes always carry the current time. What goes wrong?
hints: Where does a write with today's time land?
Sharding spreads load only if the key spreads writes.

choices.label: Adding a shard moves almost every key, as it does with key mod N
All new writes land on the latest shard, a hot spot
Old months cannot be read, because their shards are read-only
Nothing, because ranges spread writes evenly over time

acceptedIdeas: All new writes land on the latest shard, a hot spot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All new writes land on the latest shard, a hot spot

questions.onCorrect: Hashing a key such as the user id spreads writes over all 8 shards, and a range key concentrates them where the time is now.

misconceptions.feedback: That happens with a modulo rule. Ranges keep neighbouring keys together and move none when a shard is added.
Nothing makes old shards read-only. They simply receive little traffic.
They spread data over time, but writes all arrive at the present, which falls in one range.

questions.prompt: A network failure splits a replicated system in two. Which of these behaviours keeps answering and may return stale data, and which refuses some requests and never returns stale data?
hints: During the split, does the system answer or refuse?
If it answers, it may be out of date.

bins.label: Keeps answering, and may return stale data
Refuses some requests, and never returns stale data

items.label: A shopping cart that accepts items on whichever replica the customer reaches, and merges the copies later
items.explanation: Every request is answered, and the copies can differ until they are merged.

items.label: A bank ledger that rejects a transfer when it cannot reach a majority of its replicas
items.explanation: It refuses the request rather than risk two replicas disagreeing.

items.label: A news feed that shows older posts from a replica when the newest one is unreachable
items.explanation: It answers with data that may be out of date.

items.label: A lock service that returns an error rather than risk granting one lock twice
items.explanation: It gives up availability to keep the lock exclusive.

items.label: A directory lookup that answers from a local cache during an outage
items.explanation: The cache may be stale, and the answer still arrives.

items.label: A seat booking system that stops selling in the smaller half of a split network
items.explanation: It refuses sales that could double-book a seat.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cart, the feed and the directory keep answering and may be stale; the ledger, the lock service and the seat booking refuse some requests and stay exact.

questions.onCorrect: During a partition a replicated system has to choose between answering with possibly stale data and refusing, and which one is right depends on what a wrong answer costs.

flashcards.front: What is a fact about one entity, stored as a column, called?
flashcards.back: An attribute describes exactly one entity and becomes a column of its table.

acceptedIdeas: attribute
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: attribute

flashcards.front: What word names how many of one entity can relate to one of another?
flashcards.back: Cardinality is asked in both directions, so a statement about one side alone is incomplete.

acceptedIdeas: cardinality
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: cardinality

flashcards.front: What two things must be true of a noun in a description for it to become an entity?
flashcards.back: It is told apart one by one, and it has facts of its own. Anything that is only a fact about something else is an attribute.

flashcards.front: What do you call a column whose values must match a key in another table?
flashcards.back: A foreign key records the relationship and lets the database refuse a value that matches no row.

acceptedIdeas: foreign key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: foreign key

flashcards.front: What kind of table stores a many-to-many relationship as one row per pair?
flashcards.back: A junction table holds a foreign key to each side, which turns one many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many ones.

acceptedIdeas: junction table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: junction table

flashcards.front: Why is a list of ids in one column a poor way to store a many-to-many relationship?
flashcards.back: The database sees one piece of text, so it cannot check the ids, index them or join on them.

flashcards.front: What is a key called that the database generates and that means nothing outside it?
flashcards.back: A surrogate key never has to change when the real-world data does, so other tables can copy it safely.

acceptedIdeas: surrogate key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: surrogate key

flashcards.front: Which constraint refuses a row whose price is -1 when the rule is `price >= 0`?
flashcards.back: CHECK refuses any row for which its condition is false.

acceptedIdeas: CHECK
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: CHECK

flashcards.front: Why do designers put rules in the table and not only in the application?
flashcards.back: A constraint holds for every program and script that writes to the table, while an application check holds only for that application.

flashcards.front: What is an error that a table's structure invites, such as changing a fact in one row and not another, called?
flashcards.back: An anomaly comes from storing facts about several things in one table, which repeats them.

acceptedIdeas: anomaly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: anomaly

flashcards.front: What do you call a minimal set of columns that determines every other column?
flashcards.back: It is a candidate key: remove any column from it and it no longer fixes the whole row.

acceptedIdeas: candidate key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: candidate key

flashcards.front: Why can a functional dependency not be proved from the rows in a table?
flashcards.back: A dependency is a rule of the business, so sample rows can show it false with one counterexample but can never show that it always holds.

flashcards.front: What do you call rows that a join returns but that were never in the original table?
flashcards.back: Spurious rows appear when a split puts the pieces' shared column in neither key, so each side matches several rows.

acceptedIdeas: spurious rows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: spurious rows

flashcards.front: Which normal form removes dependencies on only part of a composite key?
flashcards.back: Second normal form (2NF) moves partly dependent columns to a table keyed by the part they depend on.

acceptedIdeas: 2NF
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2NF

flashcards.front: When is a decomposition guaranteed lossless?
flashcards.back: When the columns the pieces share are a key of at least one piece, so that each row on the other side matches exactly one row there.

flashcards.front: What is a table called that has one row for each event, with numeric measures and keys to descriptions?
flashcards.back: A fact table holds the numbers to add up, and its dimensions hold the words to group by.

acceptedIdeas: fact table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fact table

flashcards.front: What are the small descriptive tables around a fact table called?
flashcards.back: Dimension tables hold the who, what and when of the facts, once each, so a description change touches one row.

acceptedIdeas: dimension
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dimension

flashcards.front: Why is denormalising a decision to make after measuring and not a first step?
flashcards.back: A copy costs an update on every change and can drift, so it is only worth paying for when the reads it speeds up are measured to matter.

flashcards.front: What is the number of children each B-tree page can have called?
flashcards.back: A large fan-out makes the tree shallow, since each level multiplies the reach by that number.

acceptedIdeas: fan-out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fan-out

flashcards.front: What do you call reading every page of a table to find the matching rows?
flashcards.back: A full table scan. Its cost grows with the size of the table, whatever the query asks for.

acceptedIdeas: full table scan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: full table scan

flashcards.front: Why does an index stop helping when a query matches a large share of the table?
flashcards.back: Each matching row costs a scattered page read, so beyond a small share it costs more than reading the whole table in order.

flashcards.front: What is the share of rows that a condition keeps called?
flashcards.back: A small share is high selectivity, and an index pays off only when the share is small.

acceptedIdeas: selectivity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: selectivity

flashcards.front: What do you call an index that holds every column a query reads?
flashcards.back: With a covering index the query is answered from the index alone, without visiting the table.

acceptedIdeas: covering index
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: covering index

flashcards.front: Why can an index on `(last_name, first_name)` not seek on `first_name` alone?
flashcards.back: The entries are sorted by `last_name` first, so the entries for one first name are scattered and there is no single place to start.

flashcards.front: Which PostgreSQL command refreshes the statistics the planner estimates from?
flashcards.back: ANALYZE samples the table again, and a stale estimate is usually fixed by running it.

acceptedIdeas: ANALYZE
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ANALYZE

flashcards.front: Which two row counts does EXPLAIN ANALYZE put side by side for each step of a plan?
flashcards.back: The planner's estimate and the actual number of rows. A large gap means the plan was made from poor statistics.

flashcards.front: Why read a query plan from the bottom up?
flashcards.back: The scans at the leaves run first, and their rows flow up through the joins and sorts, so an error at a leaf is inherited by everything above it.

flashcards.front: What do you call the guarantee that all of a transaction's changes happen or none do?
flashcards.back: This is atomicity: if the transaction does not commit, recovery leaves none of its changes visible.

acceptedIdeas: atomicity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: atomicity

flashcards.front: What is the technique called of describing each change in a log before the table pages are written?
flashcards.back: In write-ahead logging the log is written first, so a commit is durable once its record reaches disk.

acceptedIdeas: write-ahead logging
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: write-ahead logging

flashcards.front: Why does COMMIT not need to wait for the table pages to be written?
flashcards.back: Recovery can rebuild the pages from the log, so the durable commit record is enough to keep the change.

flashcards.front: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?
flashcards.back: Read Committed lets each statement see data committed when it began, and allows several anomalies.

acceptedIdeas: Read Committed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Read Committed

flashcards.front: Which anomaly lets two transactions break a rule by updating different rows after reading the same data?
flashcards.back: In write skew each transaction is correct on its own snapshot, and only their combination breaks the rule.

acceptedIdeas: write skew
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: write skew

flashcards.front: Why must an application retry a transaction that Serializable aborted?
flashcards.back: The abort means the transaction conflicted with another and its changes were not applied, so running it again against the new data normally succeeds.

flashcards.front: What does multiversion concurrency control let readers do that a lock-based design would not?
flashcards.back: Readers see a snapshot of old versions, so they do not block writers and writers do not block them.

flashcards.front: Which clause added to a `SELECT` locks the rows it reads for a coming update?
flashcards.back: `FOR UPDATE` takes the row lock at the read, so a competing transaction waits.

acceptedIdeas: FOR UPDATE
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: FOR UPDATE

flashcards.front: Why is a deadlock not a bug in the database?
flashcards.back: It comes from two transactions taking locks in opposite orders, so the fix is a consistent lock order or a retry.

flashcards.front: What does a key-value store lack that a relational database has?
flashcards.back: It finds a value only through its key, so it cannot search by the content of a value without reading them all.

flashcards.front: What do you call storing child data inside its parent document?
flashcards.back: Embedding fits small, bounded data read together with the parent.

acceptedIdeas: embedding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: embedding

flashcards.front: Why does NoSQL not mean that there is no schema?
flashcards.back: The schema moves into the application, which decides what each field means, and documents written earlier keep their old shape.

flashcards.front: Without looking back, name the four ACID properties and say in a few words what each guarantees.
flashcards.back: Atomicity means all or nothing, consistency means constraints hold before and after, isolation limits interference between concurrent transactions to a stated level, and durability means committed data survives a crash.

flashcards.front: With N replicas, writes acknowledged by W and reads from R, what must hold for every read to overlap the latest write?
flashcards.back: R + W > N, because the read and write sets share a replica exactly when their sizes add up to more than N.

acceptedIdeas: R + W > N
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: R + W > N
acceptedAlternatives: r plus w greater than n

flashcards.front: Why do replicas not replace backups?
flashcards.back: A replica receives every change as faithfully as a good one, including a mistaken DELETE, and it can lag behind the primary.
